en: Preface to the Rituals for the Propagation of the Precepts:
The World-Honored One entrusted his golden brocade *kāṣāya* to Mahākāśyapa, and thus both the Dhyāna and Vinaya traditions were transmitted together.
That which is termed the "Patriarchal Seal" (*zuyin*) takes the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*—the true mark of formlessness—as the definitive purport of the three schools.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those of the Vinaya school failed to realize the fundamental principle of the mind; consequently, they split the single Dharma of the bhikṣus into five schools.
For this reason, the Chan school transmits the Dharma and transmits the mind, but does not transmit the minor vinaya.

This is because it is said that the followers of the Hīnayāna do not understand that dhyāna and vinaya share the same source, and thus they mutually revile and litigate one another. Therefore, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* takes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its fundamental principle, and through dhyāna...
One who does not understand the mind of the Dharma is called a person of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

One who, as a Dharma Master, does not recognize the discipline of the meditative mind is called one who preaches the Dharma impurely. One who, as a Vinaya Master, has not awakened to the Mind-Seal of the Chan School is called a monk who has broken the precepts.
This is because they all fail to realize that the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and the markless (*alakṣaṇa*) constitute a single school. And...
This is because, while they wished to divide the sacred grass and parcel out the land, each establishing their own ancestral shrines, they lacked the dignified bearing of a Dharma King.

Since the time of the Buddha of No-Phenomenal Marks (Amitābha), the three schools have been established and their gates opened; yet, like Rāhula dropping his alms bowl, they lack the resolve to exert themselves.
It is truly lamentable that one must once again compile this work for them. When Fazang first received the precepts at Yunqi...
Having perfected his training at Linggu, he received further instruction from Yunqi before the stupa and then taught at Yunmen;

through repeated exchanges, he unified the methods of these three houses into a single standard. This was because Zen practitioners had neglected the Vinaya while prioritizing the mind, and preceptors clung to formal appearances while neglecting the essence.
Since the ordination platform was once closed, ritual procedures have been entirely lost; people look upon one another with mutual derision and find it difficult [to practice].

I have harmonized these elements. Not presuming upon my own shallow views, I sought to recover ancient regulations and obtained the ritual for the full ordination (*upasampadā*) from the Southern Platform of former Vinaya masters.

I have briefly collated and expounded upon this, while emulating the ritual for the Bodhisattva precepts from the *Jieshu fayin* (Unfolding the Obscurities of the Precept Commentary), striving to supplement and complete it myself.

All [of these] desire that the three schools of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya be united in the single principle of the wondrous mind of Nirvana—the true mark of formlessness—so as not to fall into the harmful consequences of arrogance, impurity, and broken precepts. This is truly the painful heart of one who mends the bowl;
it is the humble view of a fellow Dharma-practitioner. Those who read this, I pray you, do not think that Chan does not interpenetrate Vinaya, nor that the Precepts do not discuss Chan.

It may be said that his treatise is a mere refutation. Consequently, he compiled the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, the Eight Precepts, the tonsure ceremony, the Ten Precepts, as well as the *Bhikṣu* *Jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and the Bodhisattva Precepts, etc., as the ritual forms for the various categories of reciting the precepts.
He further synthesized the *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya-saṃgraha*, the *Bhikṣu-śīla-mūla*, and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* as the foundational texts for the three types of recitation of the precepts, along with—
The *Sūtra of the Brahmajāla* in one volume, upper and lower fascicles, serves as the standard for bhikṣus; it is the essence of the single-minded pursuit of Chan and Vinaya.

Together with the four fascicles of the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra*, these have been carved into a single case and collectively titled the *Hongjiej fayi* (Ritual Procedures for the Propagation of the Precepts).
This is intended so that those who receive the precepts will urgently investigate Chan to seek the essence of the precepts, while those who practice Chan...
I strive to uphold the Vinaya in order to consolidate the Chan school. When Chan and Vinaya are unified in a single mind, there will be no remaining teachings that diverge from this method.
This is the primary task for addressing the urgent needs of the final age. Should there be any omissions or errors therein, I pray that those of like mind will clarify them and save me.
Recorded on the first day of the first month of winter in the Guihai year of the Tianqi era by the disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, Fazang,
at the Jinwa Hall of Beichan Temple;
a catalog of the ritual procedures for the wide propagation of the precepts.

The Ritual for Carefully Examining the Obstacles and Prohibitions for Lay and Ordained Persons Seeking to Receive the Five Precepts, the Eight Precepts, and the Ten Precepts for Tonsure and Ordination, etc.

(Extracted from the ancient manuscript of the *Jie-tan* [Precept Platform] to supplement the preceding and following texts. This ritual should be performed before receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). Furthermore, according to the Vinaya, because of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), one who is limited to only two supports loses the benefits of the renunciant life;
thus, the Buddha permitted that it may also be performed after the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
When about to ascend the platform to receive full ordination, first rectify the reception of the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*, initially receiving them from the *karmadāna* (*huangtou heshang*).
The Seventh Ritual for the Dharma Procedure (Excerpted from the Ancient Text of the Ordination Platform, with Supplemental Praise).

(From the *Supplement to the Praise* in the Ancient Text of the Ordination Platform, and the *Text for Sealing the Mind*) The Tenth Ritual:
The Method for Exhorting a Śrāmaṇera Prior to Ascending the Platform to Receive Full Ordination. (From the *Supplement to the Praise* in the Ancient Text of the Ordination Platform)

The Eleventh: The Ritual for the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of Bestowing the Full Ordination (*upasampadā*) of a Great Bhikṣu upon the Platform (Excerpted from the Ancient Manuscript of the Ordination Platform;
Supplementing the Ritual for Invoking Blessings).
Once the bhikṣu has received the full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the preceptor (*ācārya*) shall next be appointed to instruct him.

Section Twelve: The Ritual Procedures for the Characteristics [of the Precepts] (Extracted from the Ancient Manuscript of the *Jietan* [Precept Platform], including the Text for Invocation and Invitation, the Text for Opening the Path, and the Text for Conclusion; according to the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* for the conferral of the precepts).

The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion with three proclamations) is the primary ritual; the specific characteristics of the precepts emerge only after the formal enactment of the rules. Therefore, one should not recite the characteristics of the precepts upon the altar.

Furthermore, when the *upādhyāya* performs the *karman* and poses questions before the assembly, these still proceed from the mouth of the *ācārya*. How could the recitation of the characteristics of the precepts not be the duty of the *ācārya*? I hope you will not lose sight of this principle and shall instead honor the Vinaya regulations, as well as the original text for the recitation of the precepts as explained by the masters of old.

[Regarding] the various rituals for bestowing the Bodhisattva precepts: although there are certainly existing texts among the various schools within the Tripitaka, I have now [composed this] because the meaning and significance within the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* have not yet been fully elucidated.

Those who seek the precepts often understand them upon a single reception, yet they do not know what the Bodhisattva precepts truly are. Therefore, I shall now consult the sutras to establish their principles and provide repeated guidance, so that once the precepts are received, one may immediately comprehend the general significance of the Bodhisattva precepts.
This will provide profound benefit for future students; I hope you will not treat this as a mere fabrication or use it as a pretext for arbitrary interpretation.
The Thirteenth Ritual for the Bestowal of the Bodhisattva Mahā-śīla by an Ācārya Appointed to Examine the Bhikṣu [Candidate].

Therefore, it should be circulated to serve as a warning for the three types of unworthy persons.
*The Ritual for Bestowing the Three Refuges upon the Two Lay Assemblies*, Volume One of the *Extensive Ritual for the Precepts*. First: The Ritual for Bestowing the Three Refuges.

Invoking the invitation and raising the incense, I praise the inherent purity of my own mind. The nature of phenomena gives rise to light; every single thing is unimpeded—this is the Mind-King. From it, the Three Jewels emerge from their hidden storehouse.
With this single stick of mental incense, I take refuge in the majestic and open Dharma-realm of the precepts.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, such as Gandhameghakūṭa,
and other sons of noble family, upon hearing the sound of the chime, each prostrated three times and called their own names (so-and-so), then raised their hands in devout palms-joined reverence.
In inviting [the deities] and making the formal announcement:
Now, as a lotus emerges from the land, it must rely upon the nourishment of the Dharma-water; to transcend the mundane through pure mindfulness, one must depend upon the guidance of a master.
If one does not rely on the Sangha, how can one know the Dharma? If one does not take refuge in the Buddha, there is no way to escape the dust of the world. You, sirs, are currently...
(Laywoman Good Daughter), you possess the body of a Tathāgata. As you intend to shatter delusion and return to the truth, you must first abide in the secular world while following the Way.
Having already resolved to achieve perfect fulfillment and maintained a heart of profound sincerity, you have long yearned for an enlightened master and sought exclusively for the Great Dharma.

For your sake, Laywoman Good Daughter and the others, I respectfully invite Master [Name] to ascend the Jewel King Throne, respond to the capacity of this water-moon-like assembly, and expound upon the nature of selfhood.
Taking refuge. Regarding the precepts for benefiting sentient beings through instruction, the words for requesting the master should properly be recited by you yourself;
however, fearing that you may not yet be able to do so, I shall chant them on your behalf. You should follow me with utmost sincerity in making this request.

Invitation: Great Virtuous One of Brahma-like Purity, please attend with single-minded mindfulness. I, your disciple [Name], now invite you, Great Virtuous One, to serve as my primary teacher for the Three Refuges.
By relying on your great virtue, I have been able to enter the first stage. Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of compassion (one prostration).
Out of great compassion (one prostration).
The Master struck the sounding block and said:
"Since you have so earnestly extended this invitation, I shall serve as your teacher of the self-nature of the Three Refuges.
You must listen attentively to all my instructions."
"Virtuous sons and virtuous daughters, since you have already resolved your minds and taken refuge in the Triple Gem,

I shall, for your sake, respectfully invite the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Dharma-treasures of the three periods of time, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, and the successive patriarchs and monks to descend in person upon this site of practice,
to bear witness to your sincerity."
Rising to one's feet, invite the Sages. Chanting the invocation: "With incense and flowers, we invite:
Namo! With one mind, we reverently invite all the Buddhas of the ten directions, who eternally abide throughout the entirety of empty space and the Dharma-realm."

All Honored Ones of the Dharma; all Sages and Noble Sangha: We pray that you will not violate your original vows, but out of compassion for sentient beings, descend upon this site of practice and bear witness to our sincerity.

Homage! With single-minded devotion, we reverently invite the Teacher of the Land of Bliss, the Original Master of this Sahā World, the Supreme Honored One at the Dragon Flower Assembly, the Sugata of the past, present, and future (may it be as previously requested).

Homage! With single-minded devotion, we reverently invite the Great Practitioner Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion (as before). Please take your seats.
With single-minded devotion, we invoke the Dharma-protecting devas and nāgas, the assembly of holy beings of the *gārha*, and all the benevolent deities who uphold the precepts and fasts.
We pray that you will descend upon this ritual site and provide diligent, solemn protection. (Strike the wooden ruler and say: "White Words."
The Three Jewels descend in person; ten thousand deities stand guard. The Dharma-mirror of the high dais shines brightly, reflecting the heart-jewel emerging from the ocean.
It is fitting that myriad concerns be washed clean and the single wave remain unmoved, so that the mirror may contain the jewel’s luster and the jewel manifest the mirror’s radiance.

Thus, the ordinary and the sagely merge into a single source, and the host and guest shine together in dual illumination. The light of the mind is uniquely revealed, and the power of discerning awareness is complete.

Manifest! I shall now point out for you the Three Jewels of your own self-nature—the single mind and the ten wholesome paths—so that you may attain clear and thorough awakening without relying on artificial cultivation.
Thus you shall open the blue lotus within the burning house and purify white karma amidst the red dust, remaining unblemished even when ground down.

It is not blackened by mud; it is not non-existent through cultivation; it cannot be defiled. It stands in the ranks of those named "Pure" (Viśuddha) and is the most honored among lay devotees (*upāsaka*).
What is meant by "Buddha"? It is precisely this present moment of one's own mind. Like a pearl or a mirror, it is spiritually lucid and never obscured; it is clearly and constantly aware.
This awareness is without the concept of "knowing," does not rely on external conditions, and gives rise to no dualistic thoughts—this is what it is. This is what is called the Dharma.
What is this? It is precisely this very mind of non-knowing yet non-obscuration that one realizes right now; it is the original mind of all Buddhas.
One who no longer gives rise to doubt, fear, delusion, or conceptual thought is such a person. What is meant by "Saṃgha"?
It is this very awareness that is unstained, profound and unshakable, eternally pure and eternally clear, responding to conditions according to the time, like the moon reflected in water.
It is so. These are the Three Jewels of one's own mind. Because all Buddhas have realized this mind, they are called "Perfectly Awakened Ones" (Buddha).
Because all Dharmas explain this mind, they are called "Sublime Dharma" (Dharma). Because the Sangha has understood this mind, they are called the "Pure Assembly" (Sangha).
Thus, one knows that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha currently invoked are none other than the Three Jewels of one's own mind already realized. This is the first refuge.

To contemplate the manifestation of the self-mind as the Three Jewels is the realization of the present. That you are able to uphold this teaching and guide future generations so that they may clarify this mind is the realization of the future.
Thus, one knows that the self-mind encompasses the three periods of time and subsumes the ten directions;
what are called the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are fundamentally no different from one another. Once realized, it is forever realized.

All are merely empty names; that which exists is not truly existent. What is called "one mind and ten wholesome deeds" means that when the one mind does not arise, the intellect is free from greed, anger, and delusion;
the mouth does not engage in false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, or harsh words; and the body is free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Thus, the *Sutra of Forty-two Sections* says: "The mind is the chief officer (*gōngcáo*). If the chief officer stops, all the attendants cease."
Cease. Know that this very single thought of the Three Jewels of No-Mind is the fulfillment of all myriad virtues and the simultaneous manifestation of the ten perfections.

To cultivate according to this is true cultivation; to realize according to this is authentic realization. Furthermore, when combined with filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness;
benevolence, love, compassion, and harmony; the releasing of life; and the skillful means of rescuing from suffering—all these are nothing other than the extension [of this principle].
This single mind functions within the world; it is what is called the Buddha of the Mind appearing in the world.

Because this mind alone is liberated and unstained, it is the very emptiness of the nature of sin. Because this mind is pure in every thought-moment, it is the manifestation of birth in the Pure Land.
Using it for repentance, what sin will not be extinguished? Using it for the recitation of the Buddha’s name, what vow will not be fulfilled? All of these do not go beyond it.
It lies within the single mind of its own nature (*svabhāva*). Thus far, I have expounded for you the Three Jewels of your own mind, enabling you to directly realize the mind and see the nature.

Since the principle and its manifestations are now clear, the practice must be accomplished. Furthermore, you should collectively take refuge in the Three Jewels of the ten directions currently seated in the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Through the transmission of mind from teacher to teacher and the handing down of the Dharma from Buddha to Buddha, may this continue through every life and birth.
Do not turn back. You are able to take refuge; respond in accordance with the sound:
"Good man or woman, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, take refuge in the Saṅgha" (recite three times).
I take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings. I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who is free from desire.
I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the Honored One among assemblies.
(Recite three times. The taking of refuge in the Buddha is complete. The taking of refuge in the Dharma is complete. The taking of refuge in the Saṅgha is complete. (Recite three times.)
The taking of refuge in the Triple Gem is now complete. From this day forward, you shall take the Buddha as your teacher, the Dharma as your teacher, and the Sangha as your teacher;
you shall no longer take refuge in demons, heretics, or outsiders. Furthermore, I shall perform a ritual confession on your behalf.
Wash away their former defilements so that they shall not be committed again; once purified, they are forever pure. I act as the leader; you should follow in harmony.
Verse of Repentance:
All the evil karma I have created in the past Arises entirely from beginningless greed, anger, and delusion.
Whatever has arisen from my body, speech, and mind— I now repent it all.
The confession above is now complete. Furthermore, one must make a great vow to extensively deliver sentient beings and lead them all to the attainment of the Buddha-way.
First, you should seek rebirth in the Pure Land to personally behold Amitābha.

There, attaining the stage of "one-life-to-Buddhahood," you shall return to this world to transform and guide sentient beings, so that all may be born through transformation upon lotus flowers and never again wander in the cycle of saṃsāra. To this end, I shall now show you the Dharma-door of the Single-Minded Pure Land:
the six-character sacred name of Amitābha. Constantly maintain mindfulness of it and do not allow yourself to be defiled by worldly toil. Thus I say: [Recite the six characters: Namo Amituofo]
The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden (and so forth).
May I be born within the Pure Land of the West; may a lotus of the highest grade be my parents.
When the flower opens, may I behold the Buddha and awaken to non-arising, with non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas as my companions.

Having thus taken refuge in the Triple Gem, you vow to be born among the nine lotuses, to manifest as the King of Immeasurable Life, and to come as the sovereign of lands as numerous as motes of dust, never regressing and certainly attaining perfect fulfillment. You should now follow these instructions and practice accordingly.
Section Two: The Ritual Procedures for Examining Obstacles and Difficulties in Bestowing the Five Precepts for Laypersons, the Eight Precepts for the Laity,
and the Ten Precepts for Ordination,
Including the Invocation and Praise.

As soon as the true incense touches [the senses], delusive transgressions are entirely eliminated. With earnest sincerity, one pares away the wild elephant at its very inception; through profound instruction, one enters the crucible of transformation.
The substance of the mind partakes in the vast void; the wondrous precepts are fundamentally luminous.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gandhamegha-kūṭa and all the sons of good family,
upon hearing the sound of the chime, each prostrated three times, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms,
and made the formal invocation.
Pointing at the fingertip, one must see the moon; picking up the soapberry, one ought to awaken to the *jiuci* (rice-cake) offering.

Since you have received the precepts, you should first cleanse the ground of your mind before the Hall Master. Now that the *ācārya* has graced this assembly and the *chongshu chanfa* (Dharma of Repentance) is being performed, it is a matter of human propriety that you be precise and thorough.
As for the words of requesting the teacher, you should state them yourself; however, fearing that you may not yet be able to do so...
All follow my path.
To invite [the preceptor], strike the chime and chant the *brahman* melody:
"Virtuous One, please attend with single-minded mindfulness. I, disciple [Name], now invite the Virtuous One to act as my witness for the confession of the *śīla*."
Preceptor, because I rely upon your great virtue, I have been able to receive the ritual of the formal precepts and repentance. Out of compassion (one prostration).
Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of great compassion (one prostration).
The Ācārya strikes the wooden sounding-block and says:
"Have those who have not yet received the precepts departed? (The respondent leads by saying: "They have already departed. (The Ācārya says:
"O sons of good family, since you have so earnestly extended this request, I shall act as your *śīla-viniścaya-ācārya* (preceptor for the examination of the precepts)."
There is an oral instruction. Listen with a sincere mind.
The Ācārya strikes the sounding-block and says:
"One wishes to bring forth the bright moon-jewel; how could one still rely upon the defilement of mud? Since it is intended to hold the milk of a lion, it must certainly be purified."

One should wash the lapis lazuli flask. Whether one wishes to return to the precepts as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or to undergo tonsure and dyeing of robes as a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), one must in all cases abandon falsehood and return to truth, confessing and repenting for one's transgressions.
If one does not fully repent, even if one succeeds in receiving the precepts, they will still be a mixture of sin and merit, with purity and impurity intermingled.
How could such a person be a pure and singular Bodhisattva? Therefore, it is essential to be like something that has been washed clean.
Just as clothing must have its stains removed so that its original white substance can receive dye, so too must one be free of hindrances.

For humans dwelling within the six realms of existence, it is fortunate to be included among the superior ranks and to draw near to the stage of Buddhahood, making progress in cultivation easy. However, there is the fear that grave offenses may obstruct one, creating barriers to becoming a Buddha.
If there are no such obstructions, the precepts can be received. You each must, therefore, hollow out your hearts and drain your gallbladders [of deceit] before...

I shall explain each point in detail. From the past until now, regarding all that you have remembered and retained by the faculty of mind (*manas*), and all that you have done or caused to be done—such as the seven prohibitions, the ten unwholesome paths of action, and other extremely grave matters—you must disclose them to me with an open heart and exhaustively, without concealing even a single thread of it.

I shall now question you one by one; you should answer each question truthfully. Stand up individually and remain for a moment to one side, according to your respective positions. *Hu* (the ritual command).

Kneel before the Buddha. Reflect deeply and examine minutely; if it exists, say it exists; if it does not exist, say it does not exist. You must not act with a frivolous mind or allow yourself to be confused.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "If one receives the eight precepts, one must first repent for previous transgressions before receiving the precepts. As before, having received [the precepts] in sequence, one must then make a vow. The text for the vow is the same as that explained in the section on the five precepts. The Sūtra says: "If there are good men or good women who receive the precepts but do not make a vow while observing the eight precepts, they will obtain but little."

The *Kṣānti-puṇyakṣetra-jñānapāramitā-śāstra* states: Question: Between the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*) and the one-day precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*), which is superior? Answer: Due to specific causes and conditions, the two sets of precepts are equal. However, the five precepts are maintained for a lifetime, whereas the eight precepts are maintained for a single day.

Furthermore, in the case of the five precepts, the duration is long but the number of rules is few; in the case of the one-day precepts, the duration is short but the number of rules is many. If one lacks the great resolve (*mahā-citta*), then even if one maintains them for a lifetime, it is not as good as maintaining the precepts for a single day with great resolve.

It is like a weakling serving as a general: though he leads troops for a lifetime, he ultimately achieves neither merit nor fame. If, however, a hero exerts himself amidst chaos and turmoil, he establishes his merit in a single day and his fame covers the world. The comparison of the eight precepts to other precepts is likewise so. Thus says the Dharma.

From the *Yuan zhulin* (Grove of Pearls), Section on Names: Question: In the various sūtras and śāstras, what is meant by the "Eight Precepts of the Fasting Rite" (*bāguānzhāi*), and why is it also called the "Precepts of the Barrier" (*guānjiè*)? Answer: The eight precepts are so called because they close off the eight evils, preventing the arising of transgressions. Not eating at improper times constitutes the "fasting" (*zhāi*). "Fasting" (*zhāi*) means "to align" (*qí*);

it refers to restraining the six sense-faculties so as not to be defiled by the six objects of the senses, thereby aligning oneself with the severance of all evils and fully cultivating all virtues. Thus, it is named "fasting. Furthermore, the essence (*tǐ*) of fasting and the precepts is one, though their names differ. If one seeks the essence through the name, the essence may allow for slight differences:

"fasting" is named after not eating past noon, while "precepts" has the meaning of guarding against what is wrong and ceasing evil. As the *Suisheshan jing* says: "If, on the days of the six fasts, one upholds the eight precepts for one day and one night, the merit is incalculable."
[Calculation]. Regarding the six days of the *zhāi* (fasting/observance): these are the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of each month).
**The Ritual for the Ordination of a Śrāmaṇera, Part Four**:

Whenever a practitioner first receives an ordination certificate (*duò*), he shall present it upon a tray and cloth-covering to his preceptor (*běnshī*). It shall then be displayed in the respective quarters of the two orders (*liǎngxù*).

Incense. Perform three prostrations. Select an auspicious day to prepare the offerings and shave the head (according to the Vinaya, select a location and set up a seat; have the ground sprinkled with scented water in an open space, measuring seven feet in circumference).

Banners are suspended at the four corners. Nowadays, in large halls, one must face toward the Buddha, or seats may be arranged facing each other. If it is within a Dharma Hall, images, banners, flowers, incense, and candles must be set out according to the ritual. (Nowadays, in the Sangha Hall, many simple beds and seats are provided for convenience. First, perform a single prostration with contact.
Address the *raṇa* (Venerable) to harmonize the selection of the Preceptor (*śīla-ācārya*) and the Ritual Master (*upādhyāya*). The *raṇa* shall lead the invitation. The *raṇa*: [Proceeds].

Once the date for the selection has been determined, one shaves the head the night before, leaving a tuft of hair on the crown of the head (called *cūḍā*; the Sanskrit *cūḍā* means "small knot" here).
A seat and desk are prepared for the Preceptor (*śīla-ācārya*), positioned opposite the Abbot. Upon the desk are placed incense, candles, an incense burner, and a ritual ruler.
To the right of the Sacred Monk (*seng-seng*), a seat and desk are prepared for the *Vandanā-ācārya*, facing the Preceptor. Upon this desk...
The chimes for the bell are struck. On the table before the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ), place the *kāṣāya*, the *zhiduō*, and the ordination certificate (*dùdié*).
Depart from the Hall of Practice. Sound the gong to lead the tonsure candidate to the Land Deity Hall, the Patriarchs’ Hall, the Buddha Hall, and other locations to offer incense.
(Crying out: Perform three prostrations with full obeisance. Stand in line before the Sangha Hall. Ring the bell to assemble the community; the head officers and the abbot shall all enter the hall.

[The ceremony] concludes. The Preceptor and the two Karmadānas enter the hall for the first time, perform three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*), and each returns to their respective positions.

When the entire assembly is seated in unison, the Inviting Karmadāna leads [the candidate] before the Preceptor, performs three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths, and kneels with palms joined (*hukuì hézhǎng*).
(The Preceptor then asks:)

"Is the Saṃgha assembled? (The response: "It is assembled. (The question: "Is it in concord? (The response: "It is in concord. (The Preceptor says: "The Saṃgha is now in concord; what is to be done? (The response:

"To shave the head of the candidate and confer the precepts upon him. (The Preceptor says: "So be it. (He leads the petitioner to remove his sitting mat, rises, and strikes the hand-bell. He leads the person to be shaven into the hall.

After three prostrations before the Sacred Monk and three prostrations before the Preceptor, he kneels and chants the *brahman* melody. The Ācārya strikes the large bell and chants the *brahman* melody as follows):

The sages and those with the five supernatural powers, the authors of incantations, and those who possess a sense of shame—these [the Tathāgata] has gathered together, as well as those who lack shame.
The Tathāgata established the prohibitive precepts and recites them every half-month. Through the benefit of reciting the precepts, I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas.

"What is Brahma? How does one reach the ultimate further shore in this sutra? We pray that the Buddha will reveal the subtle and secret [teachings] and speak extensively for the sake of all sentient beings.
(Having finished reciting the Brahma-sutra, he said: "This is spoken for those who have shaved their heads and received the precepts.")

Raising incense, I praise the Emperor’s grace in granting me ordination; I shall not disobey His personal command. Severing the bonds of affection, I enter the unconditioned state. Receiving the Master’s Dharma according to the ritual, I shave my head and don the robes;
having received the precepts, my mind returns to its source.
The Preceptor of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has ascended the First Bhūmi rises from his seat.
The entire assembly stands together. Holding the incense burner, the Preceptor speaks these words:

"The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, the fragrance of liberation, and the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation—these clouds of radiant light pervade the Dharma-realm."
The realm: making offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, the infinite Dharmas of the ten directions, and the infinite Sanghas of the ten directions;
through seeing, hearing, and universal permeation, one realizes nirvana. All sentient beings are likewise so. This very morning, he shaved his head and received the precepts.
Opening of Merit: First, we pray that the Emperor may live ten thousand years;
that his ministers may govern for a thousand autumns; that the world be at peace; and that the Wheel of Dharma constantly turn.

May the local deities of this monastery increase in majestic radiance; may they protect the Dharma and its practitioners, ensuring that no calamities or difficulties arise. May the patrons of the ten directions be adorned with merit and wisdom.

May those assembled at the site of practice find peace and joy in body and mind. May teachers, elders, and parents excel in their spiritual cultivation. May tonsured novices proceed in their practice without hindrance.

May all beings in the three miserable realms and eight difficult conditions be liberated from the wheel of suffering. May those in the nine states of existence and four modes of birth together ascend to the shore of enlightenment.

I look up in reliance upon the Great Assembly to recite the names of the Pure Dharma-body Vairocana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
(The Great Assembly resumes their seats. The Master leads the invitation while holding the incense burner.)

Śīla-ācārya: "By relying upon the Venerable One, I have received the dharma of shaving the head and receiving the precepts.

Out of compassion... (The person shaving the head bows once; recites this a second time). "Out of compassion... (Bows twice; recites this a third time). "Out of great compassion... (Bows three times; then kneels with palms joined. The Preceptor says:)
"Good son" (the novice responds to the Preceptor, saying): "The source of the mind is profound and still; the ocean of Dharma is deep and vast.

Those who are deluded therein sink and wallow for eternal kalpas; those who awaken to it attain liberation in this very place. If one wishes to transmit the wondrous Way, there is nothing that surpasses leaving the household life.

It is as expansive and unconfined as empty space, and as pure and bright as the clear moon. When the conditions for practice are complete, the fruit of the Way is not far off. From this point on, he begins his diligent cultivation.
Through the power of such mindfulness, one ultimately realizes the stage of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One renounced the precious throne of the Golden Wheel;
at the hour of midnight, he leaped over the city walls. He cast off his precious and ornate dragon-robe and severed his hair upon the green mountains.

He allowed a magpie’s nest to rest upon his crown and permitted a spider’s web to hang between his eyebrows. By cultivating quiescence (*śamatha*), he realized the True Constant; by severing worldly toil (*kleśa*), he attained Perfect Enlightenment.

Awakened Ones! The Buddhas of the three periods have never said that one can achieve the Way while remaining a householder. Among the patriarchs of successive generations, who has ever practiced defilement while saving others?

Therefore, from Buddha to Buddha there is the passing of the hand, and from patriarch to patriarch there is the transmission of the seal. Only by remaining untainted by worldly conditions does one become a vessel for the Dharma;

thus, celestial Māras fold their hands in submission and non-Buddhists turn their hearts toward the Way. Above, this repays the fourfold debt of gratitude; below, it delivers the myriad living beings.

It is suffering. Therefore it is said that one transmigrates within the three realms and cannot abandon the bonds of affection. To enter the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) through such affection is truly to repay one's debt of gratitude.
After leaving the household life, one’s conduct transcends ordinary sentiment; one does not bow to kings, nor does one bow to parents.
"You may now leave this seat. Reflect upon the kindness of the King in providing the land and water, and the virtue of your parents in giving you life.

Pay your respects with single-minded devotion; thereafter, you shall not prostrate. (The śrāmaṇera performs one prostration. The attendant strikes the hand-chime and leads him out of the hall, saying: "Perform three prostrations facing north."

One should accept and maintain the *pātra-pātrā*, the vessel of proper measure.
Excellent are these five strips of the robe of liberation, the supreme garment of the field of merit. I now receive them upon my head;
may I never be parted from them in life after life. Oṃ siddhya svāhā.
Sevenfold is this excellent robe of liberation, the garment of the unsurpassed field of merit. I now receive it upon my head; may I always wear it throughout all lifetimes.
Oṃ dhupa dhupa svāhā.
The great robe is excellent, the garment of liberation; it is the supreme field of merit. To carry out the command of the Tathāgata, may all deluded multitudes be widely delivered.
Oṃ mahākāṣāyapaṭa siddhi svāhā.
The mantra for the sitting mat and the *niṣīdana* bedding nurtures the sprout of the mind’s nature; by unfolding it, one ascends to the ground of the sages and carries out the Tathāgata’s command.
*Oṃ damba damba svāhā* (Recite three times; the assembly likewise joins in unison until the end). The śrāmaṇera puts on the *kāṣāya* and leads the invitation, saying:

"Prostrate three times to the Original Teacher. (After the prostrations, he says again: "Prostrate three times to the Holy Saṅgha. (After the prostrations, he says again: "Prostrate three times to the Preceptor of the Precepts. (Then, he kneels in the *hu-kuei* posture.)
Join your palms. (The Preceptor says: "Virtuous son, the Dharma is like a great ocean; it becomes deeper as one enters it further.

Since you have left the household life, you must first receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts before you may become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who draws near to the Great Sangha. Out of compassion. (The śrāmaṇera recites along with the voice. The assembly joins in harmony. From "I take refuge in the Buddha" up to "out of compassion," they recite together three times. Following "out of compassion," next...)

not killing living beings; not stealing; [not engaging in sexual misconduct;

Refrain from false speech;
refrain from drinking intoxicants.

Not killing living beings;
not stealing; not engaging in sexual misconduct.

not drinking intoxicants for as long as life lasts—can you uphold these śrāmaṇera precepts? (Answer: I can uphold them.
He does not wear fragrant garlands or apply perfumes to his body;

Not eating at improper times; not handling raw gold, silver, or precious objects.

When seated, one engages in meditative reflection; when rising, one recites and chants. Thus, the three evil realms are closed off and the gate to Nirvana is opened. Within the discipline of a bhikṣu, [these qualities] increase.
Cultivate right action. Let the bodhicitta never regress. Let the wisdom of prajñā remain ever-illuminating. Widely transform sentient beings and pray for the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

With such a mind, one is a true disciple of the Buddha. (The invocation is recited: The śrāmaṇera performs three prostrations, kneels with palms joined. The Preceptor rises, holds the incense burner, and performs the dedication of merit. The Preceptor says:

Dwelling in the world like empty space, like a lotus flower unstained by water, your mind is pure and transcends even that;

and in the Saṃgha, who has stilled all disputes and entered together into the ocean of harmony.

I now invoke and request [the master] to perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

To cast off the dust of the world and depart from the secular, one should cease evil and practice compassion; to abandon delusion and return to the Truth, one must rely upon a teacher to receive the precepts.
I now request Master [Name] of such-and-such a school to serve as the *ācārya* for the Ten Precepts for you all. Moreover, this...

The Master profoundly understood the Three Contemplations and refined the Two Retentions. Regarding the Five Virtues and the Ten Recitations, he had achieved both teaching and practice; his mastery of both cessation and activity was complete.
When the request for the Master’s instruction was made, [the disciple] should have presented it himself; fearing that he might not yet be capable, he followed the Master’s lead in all matters.
[The candidate] acts as the Brahmā.
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to serve as my Preceptor for the Ten Precepts.
May the Venerable One act as my Preceptor for the Ten Precepts. Relying upon the Venerable One, I shall receive the śrāmaṇera precepts. Out of compassion, please grant this."
(One prostration) Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of great compassion (one prostration).
The *ācārya* strikes the wooden gavel and says:
"O śrāmaṇeras, since you have so earnestly extended this request, I shall serve as your *daśa-śīla-ācārya*."
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind to all these teachings.
Third, regarding the guidance provided by the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it states: "The domestic life is cramped and narrow, like a prison; all afflictions arise because of it."
Birth is narrow, while the life of renunciation is vast and expansive, like space; all wholesome causes increase by means of it.
Nevertheless, even though this is so, if one lacks pure precepts (*śīla*), none of the various wholesome merits can arise. Therefore, one should maintain pure precepts. Thus it is said:

"Shaving the hair and donning dyed robes constitute its mark (*lakṣaṇa*); receiving and upholding the prohibitive precepts constitute its nature (*svabhāva*). Hence, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

A person who has newly received the precepts is equal to the Buddha. Inferring from this, the monastics—both monks and nuns—who have left the household life are truly a gathering of wholesome dharmas.
Now that you have already left the household life, you are called śrāmaṇeras. There are two kinds of designations for the term "śrāmaṇera."
First, those whose appearance is identical to that of a śrāmaṇera; second, those whose dharma is identical to that of a śrāmaṇera.

In the Sanskrit language, *śrāmaṇera* is translated here as "Diligent Encourager" (*qín cè*), meaning one who diligently cultivates all forms of goodness and exerts the mind and its activities. Those who have merely shaved their heads and donned the dyed robes, yet have not yet received the categories of precepts, are called "those whose appearance is identical to a śrāmaṇera.
Only when they receive the ten precepts are they designated as "those whose dharma is identical to a śrāmaṇera. Now, you are about to ascend the precious altar to receive [the precepts].
To be fully endowed with the precepts, one ought first to receive the ten precepts. Desiring to receive the ten precepts, one first prays to the Triple Gem as the venerable ones upon whom to rely;
next, one entreats the myriad spirits to act as the majestic guardians who provide stability.
Fourth, the invitation of the Venerable Ācārya:
[The officiant] takes up the incense burner and stands, chanting the *brahmā-svara*. With prostrations, he says:
"Namo! We single-mindedly and reverently invite our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, and all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time."
The Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; Mañjuśrī; Samantabhadra of Great Practice; Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of Great Compassion;
all the venerable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; the Venerable Upāli, foremost in upholding the precepts; the various devas who protect the Dharma;
and the true lords of the Kālāmas—may you all deign to descend upon this site of practice to bear witness to and receive my ordination.
Thus far, we have invited the Triple Gem to descend upon this ritual site to bear witness to the reception of the precepts.

Now, as the radiant splendor of the Triple Gem and the holy sages shines brilliantly here at this assembly, each of you should lift yourselves with diligence, prostrate yourselves with your five limbs, and maintain a single-minded focus.
I shall disclose and lay bare my transgressions, seeking compassion through repentance. If it says "so-and-so," each person should state their own name;
all other words should follow my recitation.
Fifth, the Confession:
I, [Name], with a sincere heart, confess. All the various evil karmas I have created in the past arose entirely from beginningless greed, anger, and ignorance.
"Whatever has arisen from body, speech, and mind—all this I now repent" (three times).
Sixth, the questioning regarding obstacles for the sons of the Buddha: "Now that you have finished your repentance, consider all the evil karma you have committed since beginningless time."
These do not exceed thirteen grave obstacles and sixteen minor impediments. Only when these impediments are absent is one a pure vessel, fit to receive the precepts from you.
I am unable to question you now; shortly, a teacher of instruction will be appointed upon the altar to question you one by one in a private place.
You must each answer truthfully. If you do not answer truthfully, none of you shall obtain the precepts. Now, I—
I ask you all collectively: "Good sons, have you not committed any grave offenses, minor transgressions, or prohibitions? [They reply: "No.
Seventh, regarding the taking of refuge:
Good sons and others, since there are no such prohibitions or obstacles, you have just now completed the repentance before the Three Jewels; the precepts may now be conferred.
You may receive it. I shall now perform the *karmavācanā* for the Three Refuges on your behalf, causing you to evoke the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*).
If it says "so-and-so," you should state your own name; as for all other words, follow my lead.
Dharma-self (Name), for as long as life shall last, I take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions who dwell eternally. I now follow the Buddha into the homeless life;
(Name) shall be my preceptor.
I take refuge in the Sangha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. He is my World-Honored One. Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of compassion (one prostration).
Out of great compassion (one prostration).

The eighth [section] concludes by returning to the three refuges mentioned above; this is precisely the reception of the essence. By adding three further recitations, the Dharma becomes complete. The Dharma...
I, [Name], having taken refuge in the Buddha for as long as life lasts, have now followed the Buddha into the homeless life.
With [Name] as my preceptor, the Saṃgha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One. Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of compassion (one prostration). Great!
Out of compassion, [one prostrates once].
Ninth, regarding the characteristics of the recitation of the precepts:
"O sons of good family and others, I now preside over the proclamation of the *karmavācanā* for the Three Refuges for you. You have now completed the attainment of the precepts."
I shall further explain for you the characteristics of the ten precepts, so that you may recognize their features and maintain them.
As for the names of the other rules regarding observance and violation, you should inquire of your preceptor and those who are learned in the Dharma.
Not killing, not stealing, and not engaging in sexual misconduct.
Not speaking falsely, not engaging in frivolous speech, not using double-tongued speech, and not using harsh speech;
and not drinking intoxicants for as long as life lasts—can you uphold these śrāmaṇera precepts? He replies: "I can uphold them."
Not wearing fragrant flower garlands or anointing the body with perfumes;
not engaging in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor going to witness them;
not sitting on high, wide, or large beds.
Not eating at improper times;
not grasping or holding raw gold, silver, or precious objects;
for as long as life lasts, not killing living beings, and so forth, up to not grasping or holding raw gold, silver, coins, treasures, or similar items. You—
"Can you uphold them? (They answer: "We can uphold them.
Tenth, sons of good family who listen to the teaching: I have now finished bestowing upon you the characteristics of the ten precepts. Furthermore, I shall show you the five virtues.

Ten people, being robust and joyful in their aspiration for the Way, relied upon and practiced it accordingly. Their wisdom increased, they achieved eloquence, and they transformed sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
Regarding the "five virtues," the *Futian jing* (Sutra on the Field of Merit) states: first, the resolve to leave the household life.

First, because they cherish and wear the Way, they destroy their physical beauty. Second, because they accord with the dharma-robes, they do so. Third, because they have forever severed affectionate ties and are free from partiality or aversion, they do so.
Fourth, because they entrust and cast aside their bodies and lives to honor and revere the Way, they do so. Fifth, because they resolve to seek the Mahāyāna.
In order to deliver sentient beings, the number ten is mentioned. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: first, all sentient beings depend upon food for sustenance;

second, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); third, the characteristic of sensation (*vedanā*); fourth, the Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*); fifth, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); sixth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*);
seventh, the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-sambodhyaṅga*); eighth, the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*); ninth, the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*); tenth...
This is the entry into all bases of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*). This is the dharma of a śrāmaṇera; it should be thus.
Good son, having understood this, you should always keep it firmly in mind. After a short while, he ascended the precious altar before the seats of the masters.
Through the fourfold *jñapti-karman*, he received the full bhikṣu precepts, entered the ranks of the Triple Gem, became a prince of the Dharma, and succeeded to the holy lineage. His...
How vast is this benefit! From this point forward, may you cultivate diligently the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom; study the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras;
seek the fruit of Buddhahood above and transform sentient beings below; benefiting both self and others, so that the Buddha-Dharma may long abide in the world.

"May you cause sentient beings to maintain unbroken right faith. All of you, speak in unison: 'We shall practice in accordance with the teachings. (The response is: "We shall practice in accordance with the teachings.
(Recite this three times; respond three times. Descend from the seat.
Regarding the ninth procedure for bestowing the full ordination (*upasampadā*), which first appoints a preceptor (*śikṣādātṛ*) and teaches the methods for receiving the robes and the alms bowl:
The verse of invocation and praise says:
"The alms bowl is round, its cover paired; the rules for clothing are square and constant. The twenty-five items are complete; the True Dharma is upright and dignified. Within this..."
Manifesting and displaying this, he clearly demonstrates that it is not to be held [as a worldly object].

Adorning himself with the fragrance of blue lotuses, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, śrāmaṇeras, and others who have inherited the robe and bowl hear the sound of the chime. Each prostrates three times, then kneels on their right knees with palms joined.

To understand the origins of the robe and bowl, one must rely on the instruction of an enlightened master; to realize the wondrous function of receiving and maintaining them, one must depend on the exposition of a patriarchal craftsman.
I pray that you will grant your compassion and graciously accept this earnest request.

I now petition for Master [Name] to serve as your *ācārya* for the maintenance of the robe and the teaching of the bowl. Furthermore, this master is widely proficient in the Vinaya studies and has extensively investigated...
Master Zichi deeply understood the proper dimensions of robes and was well-versed in the regulations for alms bowls.

He tirelessly exhorted others toward compassionate mindfulness and skillfully engaged with sentient beings for their benefit. Regarding the request for the Master’s words, you ought to state them yourself;
however, fearing that you may not yet be able to do so, I shall chant and lead on your behalf. You should maintain sincere devotion and follow my guidance.
Strike the chime to invite [the preceptor] and chant:
"Virtuous One, attend with one-pointed mind. I, [Name], now request the Virtuous One to serve as my *ācārya* for the instruction on robes and the bowl.
May the Virtuous One act as my *ācārya* for the instruction on robes and the bowl. Relying upon the Virtuous One, I shall receive the robe."
The Ritual for the Alms Bowl. Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of great compassion (one prostration).
The Acharya strikes the wooden sounding-block and says:
"O sons of the Buddha, since you have so earnestly extended this request, I shall act as your preceptor for the receiving of robes and bowls (*cīvaradhāraṇa-pātradhāraṇa-ācārya*).
Listen with a sincere mind and attend closely to all my instructions."

Now, the cutting and sewing of the three robes were personally proclaimed by the Golden Mouth of the Tathāgata; the receiving and maintaining of the single bowl is the essential vessel for sustaining the body of a Śākya son.
Their dyed color transcends worldly garments, and their standardized dimensions distinguish them from ordinary people.
Those who wear them find their forbearance redoubled; those who maintain them become fully endowed with merit. Their value exceeds that of the seven precious jewels; it is difficult [to attain].
Its merit may be measured as being as high as a ridge of ten thousand *ren*. How could one possibly gaze up at it?
Hundreds of thousands, millions, and billions of humans and devas all bow their heads in reverence; the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths do not even know its name.
Thus, those who hear or see it receive boundless benefit; may those who uphold it find benefit for both themselves and others. Such being the case, our Buddha appeared in the world and manifested...
This is a marvelous phenomenon. It is said: "The three robes and one alms bowl are the requisites for sustaining the body.
Those who rely upon and uphold them shall ascend the gate of perfect enlightenment and proceed toward the fruit of Bodhi. From this point it began; thus, the truth is not false.
One must know that the length and breadth of the three robes, as well as the dimensions of the single alms bowl, cannot be understood without being revealed and explained. Otherwise—
By proclaiming this, one can surely know its source. Now, I shall confer upon you the Great Precepts (*mahā-śīla*). First, I will show you the names and characteristics of the robes and alms bowl;
you should take note of them. Within each of your bundles, there is a five-strip robe (*pañca-vīci-cīvara*);
in Sanskrit it is called *antarvāsa*, which here is translated as "work robe. The seven-strip robe worn upon your bodies is, in Sanskrit, called *uttarāsaṅga*. This...
Regarding the entry into the assembly of robes: each of you has a *saṃghāṭī* (Sanskrit; here translated as "variegated robe") within your bundles.
As for this *saṃghāṭī*, there are many different types, categorized into three groups of three, making nine grades in total. Among these, the lower three grades of Dharma robes are as follows:
the lowest of the low grade consists of nine strips; the middle of the low grade consists of eleven strips; and the highest of the low grade consists of thirteen strips. This...
Regarding the three grades of the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*): the lowest grade of the great robe consists of two lengths and one shortness;

it is to be maintained as a cut-and-sewn garment (*khaṇḍa-cīvara*). As for the middle three grades of dharma-robes: the middle-low grade has fifteen strips, the middle-middle grade has seventeen strips, and the middle-high grade has nineteen strips.
These three grades of dharma-robes each consist of three lengths and one shortness; they are to be maintained as cut-and-sewn garments. As for what was said...

Regarding the three grades of superior dharma-robes: the superior-inferior grade consists of twenty-one strips; the superior-middle grade, twenty-three strips; and the superior-superior grade, twenty-five strips.
Each consists of four lengths and one short piece, held as a *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (cut-and-sewn robe).
These three robes are called the *puṇya-kṣetra-cīvara* (field-of-merit robe). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The Buddha was at the entrance of the Śakra Cave in Rājagṛha."
While walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), he saw the ridges of the rice paddies clearly demarcated. He said to Ānanda, "The robe-patterns of the Buddhas of the past were like this.
From now on, let the robe-patterns be fashioned according to this. Thus, the Master of the *Zenghui* commentary says:

"Just as the fields of the paddies hold water to grow fine seedlings that nourish the physical life, so too the field of the Dharma-robe is moistened by the waters of the four benefits, thereby increasing its three [qualities]."
It is the sprout of goodness, for it nourishes the wisdom-life of the *dharmakāya*. Regarding the etymology of the term: that which is worn on the upper body is called *yi* (clothing).

"Clothing" (*yi*) means to cover; thus, clothing serves to shield one from cold and heat. Both the *sūtras* and the *vinayas* refer to it as *kāṣāya*. According to the *Zhendi zájì* (Miscellaneous Records of Paramārtha), in foreign capitals and cities, the name *kāṣāya* contains many meanings.
It is sometimes called the "dust-detaching garment" (*li chén fú*), because it severs the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Or it is called...
The "Emaciated Robe" (*kṣāma-vastra*): so named because it cuts off afflictions (*kleśa*). It is also called the "Lotus Robe," because it is free from defiled attachment.

It is also called the "Intermediate Color Robe," because its color conforms to the Dharma; this refers to what is now known as the "dyed robe" (*kaṣāya*). It is also called the "Robe of Compassion" and the "Robe of the Field of Merit" (*puṇyakṣetra-vastra*).

The *Jietan tu jing* (Diagram Sutra of the Ordination Platform) states: "The five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) cuts off greed, which pertains to the body (*kāyakarma*). The seven-strip robe (*saptakaṣāya*) cuts off anger, which pertains to speech (*vākkarma*). The great robe (*saṃghāṭī*)..."
It severs delusion; this is the mental action (*manas-karman*). Now, regarding these three robes: why not increase them by four or decrease them by one?

Why are there only three? It is because odd numbers belong to Yang; Yang can give birth to the myriad things. Now, the manufacture of the three robes symbolizes the production of the myriad virtues and the principle of taking up benefit.
Furthermore, that the long [robes] are many and the short ones few symbolizes the increase of the noble and the decrease of the ordinary. As for the color, it is dark blue-black wood.
The three colors of the orchid represent the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. As for the material, one must use mature ramie cloth;
one must not use fine, delicate items such as brocade, gauze, or silk. Therefore, our patriarch, the Holy Master of Nanshan, said: "Coarse and rough ramie and hemp shall serve as the substance.
The hair of beasts and the mouths of silkworms harm living beings and violate compassion; even if these were obtained and already finished, they must be cut up and used for plastering walls."
It is further said: "I have also seen the Indian monks who came from the West; they all wear cotton cloth (pāṭa), and thus [the sitting mat] is made only of cloth, with no other materials permitted.
What you now use as a sitting mat is called *niṣīdana* in Sanskrit, which here means 'cloth for the feet' (*suizuyi*); in the language of Tang, it is called a 'reclining mat' (*fujju*)."
It is also called a foot-cloth (*pāda-vastra*). The *Jietan tu jing* (Diagram Sutra of the Precept Platform) states:

"Just as a stupa has a foundation, your body now receiving the precepts is itself a stupa of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*). This is because the fivefold Dharma-body arises from the precepts.

Regarding what is called the *pātra*, the Sanskrit term is *pātra*, which here means "a vessel of appropriate measure. This refers to its substance, color, and dimensions, all of which must conform to the regulations.
Regarding the material: the substance consists of two things, iron and ceramic tile. Regarding the color: use crushed sesame seeds and almonds as a coating.
Both the interior and exterior are treated by fumigation with bamboo smoke, producing the colors of pigeons or peacocks. For what purpose is this fumigation performed?

To prevent food from fermenting when stored during the summer and to prevent it from becoming stained or greasy. Because it possesses these functional benefits, it must be treated by fumigation. As for its dimensions: it is the upper bowl (*uparibhājana*).
The upper bowl is one *dou*; the lower bowl is five *sheng*; the medium-sized bowl is seven and a half *sheng*. This refers to the *dou* measure of the Zhou dynasty under King Ji.
If calculated according to the Tang *dou*, the upper bowl is one *dou* and the lower bowl is five *sheng*; the medium size may be inferred accordingly.

These robes and this bowl are the primary conditions for your receiving the precepts and are essential necessities for sustaining the body; you must provide for them yourself. Whether by borrowing or by lack, [you must not rely on others].
Both are termed illegal. According to the Vinaya, it is clearly judged that in both cases one does not obtain the precepts. For a lifetime, one has received the offerings of the faithful in vain;
in the future, one will fall into the three miserable realms and undergo constant saṃsāra through kalpas, without liberation. Good son, listen: at the time of donning the robes...

Purify body, speech, and mind; with a sincere heart, receive [the teachings] upon the crown of your head. Recite mantras and chant verses. Next, unfold and arrange your robes. When eating congee or attending a meal, sit upright and spread your mat.
Join your palms and chant verses. Unfold and spread out your sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). With light hands, take up the bowl and place it in order.
After filling it with food, hold the bowl with your left hand and support the *teng* (a wooden stand) with your right. Maintain an upright posture and right mindfulness as you make the offering.
Sustain the Triple Gem. With sincere resolve, perform the contemplations; then, use the spoon to take food. Thus, the Patriarch said:
"Do not violate the five contemplations; observe moderation with the three scoops. As instructed above, receive and use robes and bowls according to the Dharma.
If you do not follow this practice, the transgression will be passed on to future generations. All the words and phrases regarding the teachings for holding robes and bowls follow my path.
The Preceptor recites:
"I bestow this five-strip *antarvāsa* robe—one long and one short—upon you.
I bestow this seven-strip *uttarāsaṅga* robe, a cut-and-sewn garment consisting of two longs and one short, for you to wear."
Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind: I, [Name], offer this twenty-five-fold *saṃghāṭī* robe— measured as four spans long and one span wide— and this *pātra*,
a vessel of appropriate measure for regular use,
as well as this *niṣīdana* mat of appropriate measure, which I now accept and maintain.
[The Master] strikes the sounding board and says:
"The secret essence of the mind-to-mind transmission of the thousand Buddhas consists solely of the Dharma and the robe-bowl.

As for the Dharma, it is the mind itself and cannot be transmitted or received. That which can be passed down requires a sign to serve as proof. This 'Dharma of sealing the mind' is precisely what is present now—"
This is the Ancestral Teacher’s Chan (Zen) that one studies. "Chan" is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term *dhyāna*, which here means "cultivation through contemplation.
Cultivation through contemplation refers precisely to the present practice of investigating the *hwadu* while giving rise to the state of doubt.
Chan possesses three meanings, namely: *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*. *Śamatha* means that form is fundamentally empty, as it lacks any substantial entity. Three...

"Mā" refers to that which is fundamentally empty yet exists as an illusion, being established through dependence on conditions. To know it as empty while failing to understand its conditional nature is called "one-sided emptiness.

To know its conditional nature while failing to understand its emptiness is called "chasing after existence. When one simultaneously embraces both emptiness and existence, and within existence itself embraces emptiness, [this is the Middle Way].

This is called "confused and evasive. To say it is neither empty nor existent is called "falling into negation. To transcend both affirmation and negation, and to be both is and is not—this is what is spiritually realized and made luminous.
It is given a provisional name, "Dharma," which is both most manifest and most esoteric; therefore, it is called the "Mind Seal" (Cittamudrā). This alone is that which Buddhas transmit and receive.
However, the mind cannot be transmitted to others, and the Dharma cannot be characterized by continuity or interruption; therefore—
The transmission of the Dharma is situated within the context of the transmission of the robe and bowl; this shall now be clearly elucidated.

The bowl is hollow within and solid without, circular in shape, and composed of two parts joined together. These two parts intersect, symbolizing the shaven crown of a monk, corresponding to Heaven and the Two Polarities (the Earth).
It contains immeasurable subtle meanings and produces immeasurable merit and virtue, serving as a symbol for fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). As for the robe, its exterior is square...

Internally penetrating, it distinguishes the breadth and narrowness of its sections; long and short, it is cut and shaped according to the Dharma. It manifests existence and attachment, embodying both the orthodox and the heterodox like the monastic community.

Its body responds to the earth while simultaneously encompassing all things—like the flourishing of crops in a field, or like water flowing to nourish and moisten. This serves to symbolize the wisdom of differentiation.

Generally, when one first attains great enlightenment through Zen meditation, one immediately acquires fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is perfectly complete and wondrous, wherein all phenomena are fully present.
When one’s realization is sufficient and becomes undifferentiated, upon receiving the Dharma from a teacher, one attains discriminative wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Reaching the point of analysis, the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*) unravel thread by thread and dissolve into clarity. Thus, one first attains fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and subsequently enters into subsequent wisdom.

Only then does one correspond with the robe and alms bowl. If one attains only fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) but not discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), it is like a monk holding an alms bowl while remaining naked.

If one attains only discriminative wisdom but has never undergone great awakening, then that fundamental self-awakened noble wisdom (*svasaṃvedya-āryajñāna*) is like a person wearing a cap and gown while starving to death.
Therefore, the Buddha prescribed the robe and alms bowl; for even a moment, one must not be separated from them.
To be "separated" means to be temporarily absent, like one who is as good as dead. Therefore, those who wish to become bhikṣus must possess their robes and alms bowl;
the Dharma must be realized by oneself and cannot be borrowed from others. This is why the monastic community speaks of "grass sandals," calling them "borrowless grass sandals.
If even these are called "borrowless," how much more so the Buddha-Dharma? Yet, some rely solely on borrowing it from their teachers.
...yet do not seek to personally attain awakening through direct realization? Therefore, those who transmit this bowl treat it as if they were holding the crown of the Buddha’s head;
if they touch it so that it makes a sound, as if striking the Buddha, they incur the same offense. This is because the Dharma is revered.

By day, one carries it for alms to nourish the life of wisdom, causing the donor to cultivate merit upon the crown of the Buddha’s head. By night, one rests the head upon it to manifest one's own [realization].

The head is without marks; it is identical to the markless crown of the Buddha’s head. Since one’s own head cannot be separated from oneself, the alms bowl cannot be separated [from the practitioner].

Just as a person cannot be without food for a single day to sustain their life, so too the bowl cannot be separated. Since one’s own head cannot be left alone, the bowl must not be touched [carelessly].
Just as a person cannot have their head injured for even a moment or an instant, so it is with the bowl. As it is with the bowl, so it is with the robes and deportment.
Indeed, this may be inferred by analogy. Those who are bhikṣus are the seed of the Buddhas who transmit the mind-seal (citta-mudrā). Therefore, they shave their heads and carry alms bowls;
they purify their bodies and don robes. This Way must not be abandoned for even a moment. The mendicant’s staff (khakkhara) is the emblem of the True Dharma.
Gold is used for its pliability, and tin for its brightness and purity; it is hollow within and solid without. As for gold, it is one of the five elements (pañca-dhātu).
Its height represents the supreme dignity of the Dharma. Its flexibility represents the Dharma-gate’s emphasis on forbearance. Its clarity and purity represent its imperviousness to defilement.

Being hollow within and solid without represents the clear distinction of the Middle Way. Adorned with the Four Truths and the Six Perfections, it is upheld by the two contemplations within a single mind.
It does not allow for attachment to the ground, as there is nowhere to abide; nor does it allow for separation from its sides, as it cannot be parted.

It is abandoned. When lying down, one sleeps together with it; when walking, one goes together with it; when standing, one leans against it. This is the method of "the staff before one and the crossbar leaning behind.
How solemn is this method! It must not be turned away from. How venerable is this method! It must not be touched. To distance oneself from it is to turn one's back on it;
to approach it is to touch it—both are extreme views. A bhikṣu should properly shoulder this burden and not cast it aside, day by day.
This is the ultimate purpose. It is for this reason that the robes, alms bowl, and mendicant’s staff were established.
To carry the hand-towel, water flask, and cleansing powder together is to attend to the purification of the body. The use of the willow branch is to purify the karma of speech.

As for the carrying of the razor, it does not merely sever the afflictions of the three poisons; it is the Vajra King’s sword, by which all phenomena at the very root must be decisively cut off. The tweezers...
The use [of these implements] is to extract the thorns of views. Carrying the water-purification flask is to sprinkle the rain of the Dharma.

The sutras, the vinaya, and the Buddha-image represent the Three Jewels being fully present within one’s own mind. Sitting and reclining upon the rope bed signifies being unstained like a lotus flower.

Eating a single meal at midday symbolizes that the sustenance of the body relies on a single dharma—neither two nor three—and does not exceed the Middle Way. Lodging for a single night under a tree...
The alms bowl signifies having no home or livelihood. Holding the incense burner signifies practicing the fragrance of the precepts. The water strainer signifies practicing the conduct of compassion.
The fire-starter symbolizes that the mind must have neither fire nor lack of light. These are the indispensable requisites for a dhūta practitioner wandering abroad to transform and guide others;
they are none other than meditation and discipline. When the dharma implements are complete, the Buddha-way is accomplished.
This is indeed something that must be clarified for the sake of Kai. It must not be neglected.

To carve and polish all the various features depends entirely upon the skill of a master craftsman; to educate and bring forth a person of complete talent requires the power of an enlightened teacher.
If one does not reverently invite such a person, how could one follow them for long?
Now, for your sakes, we single-mindedly and respectfully invite Master [Name] to serve as your *adhiṣṭhāna-ācārya* (empowering preceptor). Moreover, this teacher never tires of instructing others.

These are divergent paths. When they meet, they strike their palms in approval; yet those who truly possess such realization are rare. The Layman Lu carried out his grain-pounding and attained perfection right where he was;
