Since they have become lost on the main thoroughfare of entering the Way, he specifically reveals the narrow path of leaving the household life. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:

"If there are those who do not recognize the dharma of leaving the household life, who delight in and cling to birth and death, and do not seek liberation from them—for this reason, the Bodhisattva renounces his kingdom and wealth."
He left the household life to seek tranquility; though entangled by the five desires, he did not remain at home.
Because he wished to bring sentient beings to liberation, he manifested a lack of delight in dwelling amidst the five desires, and thus left the household life to seek tranquility.

By this it is known that those who seek the Noble Path must first leave the household life. Thereupon, manifesting his traces in Central India, he leaped over the city wall at midnight, urging on his white horse.
Ascending into the void, he went to the azure clouds to cut his hair. Once the thunderous voice had resounded, the "Welcome" (Svāgata) formula first initiated the five men.
As soon as the rain of Dharma moistened the earth, the *karmavācanā* rituals flourished throughout the four seas. To this day, all people receive its bounty.

O sons of good family, you possess roots of merit from past lives; having encountered the Buddha’s grace, you have attained the perfect marks of a monk and ascended the altar to receive [the precepts].
Regarding the precepts: one does not know the meaning of the precepts, what dharma constitutes their practice, how they are received, and once received, how they are upheld.

Furthermore, what are the characteristics of upholding and violating them? If one is deluded regarding these essential points, one will merely have the name of ascending the altar to receive the precepts, yet lack the actual substance of receiving them;
thus, one’s entire life will be spent in vain, remaining in essence a layperson. Therefore, I—

Before you receive the precepts, I shall elucidate for you the fourfold meaning of the nature and characteristics of the precept-substance (*śīla-dhātu*), so that your minds may attain clarity and you may thoroughly understand the Dharma of the precepts.
As you engage with all sensory objects, direct your mind to receive them, internalizing the substance without contradiction.

I shall then demonstrate how to unify the mind and give rise to the ritual forms based upon that substance, so that your deportment may be worthy of observation in the midst of daily activities; only then should you ascend [to the platform].
At the altar, one receives [the precepts] according to the conditions, so that the essence of the original reception may be maintained as a manifest vow for the rest of one's life.

One gives rise to various ascetic practices and distances oneself from all transgressions, thereby restoring the originally pure mind. This pure mind is inherently possessed from the beginning; it does not depend on cultivation or effort, nor does it fall into the categories of existence or non-existence.

It is neither non-existent nor non-non-existent, nor is it the negation of that negation. Even the state of "not forgetting" is transcended, severing all names and words, beyond the reach of conceptual thought.

Abiding therein with spontaneous non-obstruction is called the pure mind; it is also termed the essence of precepts (*śīla-sarīra*). To employ this pure mind to direct one’s thoughts is called "conditioning the object.
To receive [the teaching] with this pure mind is called "receiving the precepts. To maintain and protect [the teaching] with this pure mind is called "upholding the precepts.
When one's practice accords with this, it is called the "characteristic of the precepts" (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*). That which is called the "dharma of the precepts" is precisely the Buddha.
That which is regulated consists of the prohibitions and defenses against the three poisons; these are the thirty thousand and eight thousand immeasurable codes of discipline (*vinaya*).

As for what is called the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-svabhāva*), it refers to one’s own mind universally taking as its object all things, both sentient and insentient, as well as the infinite realms of the two truths—emptiness and existence—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Regarding all objects of experience, one gives rise to three kinds of resolve. First, the resolve to vow to sever all evil—namely, the non-virtues of body and speech such as lust, theft, killing, and lying—and to bring all faults to a complete halt.
Because success is achieved through this severance, it is called the "Virtue of Severance" (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
In the future result, one realizes the Buddha of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Second, the resolve to vow to cultivate all goodness—namely, that which is mundane and supramundane...
Regarding all wholesome dharmas in the world, one practices them through skillful means; there is no virtue that is not cultivated.

Virtue is cultivated by means of wisdom, and success is achieved because of virtue; this is called the "Virtue of Wisdom. In the future, upon the attainment of the fruit, one realizes the Buddha of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Third is the vow to deliver all sentient beings. The previous two vows were practices for one's own benefit; now, one universally delivers all conscious beings, causing them all to attain [enlightenment].
The unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood—bodhi and nirvana—is the practice for the benefit of others. Bestowing grace upon all things is termed "gracious virtue.

Upon the attainment of the future fruition, one realizes the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. When the mind takes an object as its condition, the object manifests from the mind; the object is itself the essence of reality (dharmatā).

The essence is itself the cause of the precepts. Prior to receiving them, this essence is unconditioned (*anupādāna*). When one grasps the dharmas within this essence, relying upon one's own mind, the precepts serve as the dependent and the mind serves as the basis.
The harmonious integration of the mind and its mental factors is termed the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-svabhāva*), analogous to the metaphor of a medicinal pill.

One can know this through the three types of *śīla* (precepts). As for the practice of *śīla*, it refers to the practitioner relying on the essence of their original vows and engaging in various activities throughout the course of daily life;

this is called the practice of *śīla*. Regarding what is termed the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of *śīla*, it is as detailed in the various codes of discipline, which clarify the characteristics of upholding and violating the precepts.
This is precisely the characteristic of the Dharma. Within the four modes of deportment and the daily activities of life, this is the manifestation of its practice.
If you all understand the Dharma in this way and uphold it accordingly, you will perhaps accord with the sacred virtue and truly be children of the monastic community who maintain the Dharma.

It is solely the planting of the seed of Bodhi; it looks to the precepts and Vinaya to take root.

Truly, they serve as the embankment for the True Dharma and shall forever act as the moat and rampart for the Citadel of the Mind-essence. Without relying on external protection, how could its wide propagation be made secure?
For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests as a Wheel-Turning King to bring about governance.

The sovereign has opened the way for the Buddha’s transformation to proclaim its majesty. Observe how the successive rulers of India protected and promoted [the Dharma], and how the accumulated dynasties of China issued imperial edicts to propagate it.

How much more so for our Sagely Court, where the sun of wisdom shines brightly and the breeze of benevolence fans far and wide; having inaugurated the altar in the tenth year of Hongwu, and continuing this noble tradition...

During the reign of Emperor Chengzu, Emperor Shenzong bestowed robes and a dharma-staff upon him at Mount Wutai, whereby the Vinaya was restored and the monastic communities (senglin) beheld him as a sun and moon within the three realms, illuminating the Dharma once more. though I am deeply ashamed of my own worthless wood, I seek to repay this great bounty by sincerely inclining my heart like a sunflower toward the light.

I pray that the Dharma of the Precepts may flourish forever, and that I may offer eternal blessings to the Heaven of Yao. With reverence, I prepare this altar of the wild weeds and study to unfold the Vinaya of the Sūtra. May it spread boundlessly—

One makes a solemn vow that both the sensory realm and the self shall be simultaneously stilled, so that the virtuous faith of the ten directions may pour into your body and mind.
The five parts are established as the foundation; the three bodies are fully endowed. One must share the same resolve; may there be no divergent conditions. (Name) respectfully informs you.

The Fourth: The Dharma Concerning the Location Where the Precepts Are Received. (The Buddha said:

"The person receiving the precepts must not be in an empty or hidden place that is beyond the range of sight or hearing. Turning around to face west, he descends from the altar. The attendant goes to the place of the *śāstr* (preceptor) and spreads out a seat. "Good son, the masters upon the altar are performing the ritual and have dispatched me down here to inquire of you three regarding obstacles and impediments.
Do not be afraid. In a brief moment, I shall cause you three to ascend the precious altar, receive full ordination, become great bhikṣus, and enter the ranks of the Triple Gem.
This is no small matter; you should feel profound joy."
Now, the precepts are the very root of Bodhi and the foundation of the Noble Path. In the Buddha’s world, when conditions were favorable, a single movement would immediately evoke a response.
In this degenerate age of the Dharma-ending period, the Sage’s regulations follow conditions: when conditions assemble, the ritual is performed and success is achieved;

when conditions disperse, the virtue of the precepts cannot be established. The merit of non-action (*avijñapti*) is invisible; its presence or absence is determined by reliance upon conditions. [This applies to] the three robes...

This single bowl is the primary condition for the three of you to receive the precepts. Before I inquire of you regarding the prohibitions and obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*), I shall first explain to you the names and characteristics of the robes and the bowl;
you should understand this. Within each of your bundles, there is a five-strip robe (*pañcaka-vastra*);
in Sanskrit it is called *antarvāsa*, which here means a "work robe. It is used for performing labor and service within the monastery, as well as while on the road...
When entering, staying, or returning, you should wear this robe. The seven-strip robe worn on your bodies is called *uttarāsaṅga* in the Sanskrit language;

here it is translated as the "robe for entering the assembly. Whenever you attend a meal or a lecture, perform repentance or recite scriptures, prostrate to the Buddha or practice seated meditation, or engage in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* ceremonies, you should wear this robe.
Within each of your three bundles, there is a *saṃghāṭī* robe. In the Sanskrit language...
*Saṃghāṭī*. This is translated as the "Patchwork Robe" (*zàsuì yī*). It refers to a garment made from cut and pieced fragments, so called because it consists of many strips.
Whenever one enters a royal palace, ascends a seat to preach the Dharma, goes on almsround in a village, or subdues non-Buddhists by manifesting majestic power, this robe must be worn.
Each of you three has one *pātra*. In the Sanskrit language it is called *pātra*; here it is translated as the "Proportionate Vessel. As for its substance...

The three dimensions of form are all in accordance with the Dharma. Furthermore, these robes and bowl are the insignia of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and the standard observance of the noble Śramaṇas.
Among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths in the Western Heavens, they do not even know their names;
it was only the World-Honored Buddha who revealed this unprecedented teaching. Now that you have obtained and received them, you must—
"Revere, respect, and cherish it. However, these robes and bowl must be procured by yourself; if they are borrowed or not your own, they are termed 'unlawful.
Now, do you three already possess these robes and bowls? [They] replied, "We already have them. [The Teacher] said, "Excellent."

"Listen, son of good family. Since beginningless time, you have given rise to a false and delusive mind, deceiving the sages and worthies, sinking into the cycle of birth and death with no prospect of liberation.
Now that you have sought refuge in the Buddha and left the household life, you are a disciple of the Buddha and have received the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts."
To cross the ford of birth and death, one must strive to sever the root of false delusion and practice the path of reality; this is precisely the time for sincere resolve.
I now ask you regarding grave prohibitions and minor obstructions. You should carefully examine this body: if it exists, say it exists; if it does not, say it does not.
If you do not understand or recognize [the answer], you must not give a false reply. Of you three, first of all, have you never committed a transgression against the fundamental boundaries?
I judge that you three, having only recently entered the gateway of the Dharma, do not yet recognize the names of these offenses.

Having once received the Buddha’s precepts, if you violate even one of the four root precepts—sexual misconduct, stealing, killing, or lying—you will be cast adrift upon the outer shores of the ocean of the Buddha.
One shall never again be permitted to enter the assembly of the pure, nor to participate in the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) or formal acts (*karmavācanā*);

this is called a "borderline offense" (*antimā āpatti*). Do you three truly have no such offense? [They reply: No. When you were not yet laypeople, nor when you were *śrāmaṇeras*, did you defile a bhikṣuṇī of pure conduct?
[They reply: No. When you were not yet laypeople, nor when you were *śrāmaṇeras*, did you eavesdrop on the Saṃgha as they recited the precepts? [They reply: No.
Regarding the precepts: one who falsely claims to be a bhikṣu and receives the respect, offerings, and prostrations of others is called a "thief-dweller" (caura-vāsin).
The Buddha did not permit the ordination of such a person. Are you not such a person? [He] answers: "No."
"You were not originally a non-Buddhist, but having joined the Buddha to leave the household life and received the Buddha's precepts, you returned to the non-Buddhists. Now you have come once more.
This person’s disposition is unstable; he is called one who 'breaks' both internal and external paths. He is not a vessel for the Buddha-dharma, and the Buddha does not permit his ordination."

"Are you not one of these persons? [He] answers, "No. [The five types of impotent persons (*paṇḍaka*) are: 1. **Born Impotent** (*jātipaṇḍaka*): This refers to a person who, from birth, lacks the full development of male organs. 2. **Castrated Impotent** (*kṛtapaṇḍaka*): This refers to a person whose male organs have been removed by means of a blade;

such a person is called a castrated impotent. 3. **Envious Impotent** (*īrṣyāpaṇḍaka*): This refers to one whose male organs appear to be absent, yet upon seeing another engage in sexual intercourse, envy arises and subsequently causes the organs to manifest; such a person is called an envious impotent. 4. **Transformable Impotent** (*parivartakapaṇḍaka*):

This refers to one capable of transformation. Encountering a man, he transforms into a woman; encountering a woman, he transforms into a man; such a person is called a transformable impotent. 5. **Half-month Impotent** (*pakkhapaṇḍaka*): This refers to one who is capable of being a man for half the month and incapable for the other half; such a person is called a half-month impotent. These are the five.
"Are you not a man of no seed? (He answers: "No. "Have you not killed your father or mother; have you not killed your preceptor or teacher;

have you not disrupted the Saṃgha that performs the *karmavācanā* and turns the Wheel of Dharma; or have you, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha? These are called the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*).

"Son, have you come to receive the precepts by transforming yourself into human form while being a non-human being? (He answers: "No.
"Are you one who, though not among the various dragons or animals, possesses great supernormal powers and is able to manifest transformations, coming in human form to receive the precepts?"
(He replied: "No. Within the bodies of you three persons, do you each not possess both male and female sexual organs?
(They replied: "No. "Good sons, this constitutes the thirteenth serious impediment (*guru-antarāya*). Since these serious impediments are absent, you are indeed pure vessels.

"Since you have left the household life, each of you has been instructed and guided. What is the name of this Dharma? (Each answers: 'It is [Name]').
This is the Dharma for your three of you who have entered the Way; it is the designation for your entire lives.

From now on, after receiving the precepts, whenever you see your *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, your venerable colleagues on the same platform, those of the upper, middle, or lower seats, officials, elders, friends, spiritual mentors, or your parents..."

The Ninth: Clarifying the Dharma of the Precept-essence (*śīlaskandha*).

(The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first preach the Dharma to them, guiding and enlightening them so that they give rise to compassion toward all objects; thus, they shall attain the superior precepts. "Good son, you have no grave obstacles before you and no minor hindrances behind you; you are a truly pure vessel. The Sangha rejoices together in this, and we shall confer the precepts upon you.

One must necessarily take the objective realm as a condition to give rise to the resolve; when the mind and its object are mutually compatible, one then gives rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*).

"Is it pure in the midst? (He answers: "No.

One takes refuge in the Buddha that is one's own original mind. For those of superior faculties and sharp capacities, upon hearing the two words "self-refuge," they immediately return to the root and source, thoroughly penetrating the ground of the mind. How direct and exhilarating!

These emotions and this mind all enter into the Buddha-nature precepts. Thus we know that by taking refuge once, one immediately realizes the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*).

Therefore, whether lay or ordained, one attains refuge in one's own Buddha. Having realized that my own mind is certainly not that of an ordinary being (*sattva*), I take refuge in myself.
Dharma, you already know my mind. The original transmission of the Mind-Seal has returned to its own monastic source. You already know my mind; it has never been defiled.
From beginningless time until now, it has been consistently Buddha, without ever shifting by so much as a single hair’s breadth.

It is only because of the habitual taints of the conditioned mind that one flows into killing, stealing, lust, falsehood, folly, greed, and anger, thereby causing oneself to become deluded. For example:
It is like the moon, which is originally in the water and has never been lost;

As the saying goes, "The faults of the gentleman lie within his own party," and such habits are easily perpetuated;

unaware that they have committed an offense, they fail to realize that according to the explicit judgments of the scriptures, neither group attains the precepts. This applies even to those who commit offenses inadvertently due to ignorance.

Thereupon, Śākyamuni, about to transmit this Mind-Ground, emitted a radiance (then picking up his *cintāmaṇi* staff, he said):
Listen! Is this not indeed light? This very ground of the mind (cittabhūmi) is that which cannot be proclaimed by words; therefore, it causes the Light to inform the Buddhas upon the thousand petals.

They shall take this "Chapter on the Dharma-Door of the Ground of My Mind" and go forth, causing them to receive it thus, to uphold it thus, to recite it thus, and to practice it with single-mindedness.
Thus, the thousand Buddhas cannot fathom it with their minds; for this reason—
It also emits this light, within which emanated Buddhas likewise scatter flowers as an offering.
This is like the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa smiling; it is the succession of lamp from lamp.
One enters through the point where one cannot grasp the back or touch of this light and these flowers. This essential nature is empty space; one enters and exits here within the Flower-Light Samādhi.
Yet these thousands of millions of Śākyamunis are neither two nor distinct.
It is just like the elder patriarchs throughout the world, who at the moment of death either stand transformed upside down, pass away while sitting or standing, or enter the womb and take birth;

whether they realize the Way through Zen meditation, wield the mallet and brandish the fly-whisk, or engage with sentient beings to benefit them—all of these are none other than those who sport in the supernatural powers of this samādhi and purify Buddha-lands.

Therefore, when our Śākyamuni Tathāgata descended from the celestial palaces to be born in Jambudvīpa and realized the Way through the eight phases of enlightenment, he did not depart from his Flower-Light King’s throne.
He expanded this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, which is like the net-banner of the Great Brahmā Heaven:
by means of a single mesh of the net, one perceives all the infinite meshes. Thus, the gateway of the Buddha’s teachings resides solely within this.
In an instant, one attains mastery over every dharma and every aspect; there is nothing that does not accord with this.

For the sake of the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa—those ordinary people shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—the Buddha taught that within the inherently pure and full *cittabhūmi*, one should constantly recite and practice this single precept, the radiant, indestructible diamond-like jewel of a precept. Therefore it is said: "This is all..."
This is the original source of the Buddhas and the seed of Buddha-nature; it is that which all sentient beings equally realize and equally possess.
If you can attain realization upon this "As You Wish" (Yirui), then regardless of your various consciousnesses, forms, or minds—whether they be emotional or mental—they all enter into this precept.
Therefore, at every moment there is a cause, and by means of this alone, there is the eternally abiding Dharma at every moment.
The body abides herein alone. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas receive and uphold it, never departing from this grid.
You, the great assembly, should likewise receive and uphold it; do not depart from this grid.
This is precisely your own original source-nature, pure by nature, which is called the *Prātimokṣa*. It causes people to turn their backs upon [the world] toward this very place.
Do not touch it. You must not seek awakening or penetration through this; rather, you must establish your dwelling and sustain your life right here.

If you have not yet awakened to or fully understood this, then regarding this very dharma, you will be unable to proceed either horizontally or vertically, like one who cannot reach out to grasp anything within a great mass of fire.
Naturally, you will neither touch nor transgress it; such is its power.
"Participate. Therefore it is said, "Filial and Obedient. To be filial and obedient means to be filial and obedient to this precept of the mind-ground.
It is through this that one restrains oneself; it is through this that one gives rise to function. Thus, the Buddha again emitted light from his mouth to discourse extensively upon this matter.

From ordinary beings to sages, all recite these words of the precepts. Since the light of the precepts issues forth from the mouth, there must be a specific purpose for it; therefore, it is said that there is a "condition" (pratyaya). It is not otherwise.

To claim it has no cause or that it has causes and conditions would likewise constitute a transgression. Therefore, it is called "radiance" (*ābhāsa*): it is neither blue nor yellow; it is neither matter nor mind;
it is neither being nor non-being; it is neither cause nor effect. Now, to claim it is neither cause nor effect would again constitute a contradiction. What is contrary cannot be touched.
One cannot attain awakening or achieve realization through this alone; it is simply this single point of the fundamental source from which both ordinary beings and sages arise.
Therefore, you should uphold it, recite it, and study it well. Even those who merely understand the words of the Dharma Master have fully received these precepts.
(Again, he raises his *ruyi* staff and says:)
"Good son, look and see if you understand my words. If you understand them, you are already within this very state: donning the robes and holding the bowl, go;
if you do not understand them, you are likewise within this very state: go with horizontal and vertical investigation. It does not transcend this precept.
If you do not understand, it does not transcend this precept. Therefore it is said: 'All those who possess a mind should receive the Buddha-precepts. Sentient beings receive [them]..."
The Buddha’s precepts mean that one immediately enters the rank of all Buddhas. Once one’s rank is identical to that of Great Enlightenment, one is truly a child of the Buddhas;
this itself is the precept—do not seek it elsewhere. Having finished explaining the precepts to you above, you are now no different from the Buddhas.
If, in this regard, you violate them by even a hair’s breadth or turn away from them by even a hair’s breadth, you will immediately fall into the ten grave offenses.
The forty-eight minor precepts and so forth are subsumed within the characteristics of the *prātimokṣa*. Be careful! Be careful!
Having thus far demonstrated the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Precepts, you have now completed receiving them. Nevertheless, although the Mind-Ground is clear, if one does not give rise to...

The Great Vows still belong to the stage of limited fruition. One must resolve upon the vast mind and establish the Four Great Vows before one can expand the Bodhisattva path and universally benefit all sentient beings.
I now proclaim this Way; you should now make these vows.
I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings; I vow to sever inexhaustible afflictions;
I vow to study immeasurable Dharma gates; I vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
(Chanted three times, with three responses.)
I have thus far guided you through three rounds of *karmavācanā*, causing you to give rise to great vows for the sake of inexhaustible and vast benefit. You are now fit to receive the precepts;
furthermore, I shall cause you to maintain a solemn and earnest mind so that the ritual may be completed. I reverently entreat Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva to act as the presiding witness.
Karmavācanā Master: I shall now further perform the threefold karmavācanā on your behalf. Be diligent in its completion;
receive and uphold it with reverence and care (performing the *brahman* chant).
Present Bodhisattvas, sons of good family: you who have now come before me to request that I sit upon the site of enlightenment,
seek to receive from your original teacher, the Great Preceptor Śākyamuni, the Dharma of the Bodhisattva Mind-Ground and the Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Precepts—
namely, the precept of restraining misconduct, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the precept of benefiting sentient beings.

Precepts (the three virtues being perfectly bright and complete like the worldly letter *i*): these are that which all bodhisattvas of the past have already received, studied, understood, practiced, and accomplished;
that which all bodhisattvas of the future shall receive, study, understand, practice, and accomplish;
and that which all bodhisattvas of the present are now receiving, studying, understanding, practicing, and accomplishing, destined to become Buddhas in the future.
(Directly: From this moment until you attain Buddhahood, you shall receive the precepts. During that interval, you must not violate them.
Can you uphold them? (They reply: We can uphold them.

Thus far, I have performed for you the first *karmavācanā*. The Buddhas of the ten directions emit great precious light; (first, this is used) to consecrate your body and mind with this wondrous and virtuous Dharma of the precepts.
(Second, this is used) so that the Dharma of the precepts pervades all space and gathers above the crown of your head.

(Third, this is used) so that the Dharma of the precepts enters your heart, making you inwardly and outwardly pure and fit to receive the precepts. May you, with this precept-mind, reverently uphold them in filial obedience from lifetime to lifetime.
"Be born again and again; be firm and do not retreat. This is the first and second *karmavācanā*. Having been completed once, it is repeated a second time for the sake of careful understanding.
This is the second and third *karmavācanā*.
The three rounds of *karmavācanā* have now been completed. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions grant their silent approval. Your present minds are themselves the Buddha;
you shall certainly become Buddhas in the future. Moving forward, through true inquiry and authentic realization, may you attain the Dharma and achieve correspondence with it.
The nature of constant abiding precepts is ultimately immovable; furthermore, you should now grasp their characteristics and maintain them.
I shall now explain, according to the ten characteristics of the inexhaustible precepts as taught in the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Ratnavyūha-sūtra*); listen well, all of you. The Buddha said:
O Son of the Buddha: From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entirety of the future, you must not intentionally kill during that interval.
Should you violate this, it is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva; you shall lose the Dharma of the forty-two stages of the Sages and Worthies. You must not violate it. Can you uphold this?
(He replied: “I can uphold it, Son of the Buddha.
From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entire extent of the future, during that interval, I shall not intentionally commit theft.”
If one commits a transgression, it is not the practice of a bodhisattva; one loses the forty-two dharmas of the noble ones and shall not commit such acts.
Can you uphold this? (He replies: I can uphold it.

"O Son of the Buddha, from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entire span of the future, you must not intentionally engage in sexual misconduct during that interval.
Should you violate this, it is not the practice of a Bodhisattva; you will lose the Dharma of the forty-two stages of the noble ones. You must not violate it. Can you uphold this?"
(The answer was: "I can uphold it.

Son of the Buddha, from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entire extent of the future, in the interval between them, I must not intentionally utter false speech.
If I were to violate this, it would not be the conduct of a bodhisattva; I would lose the dharmas of the forty-two worthies and sages. I must not violate it; I can uphold it."
"No. (The respondent says: "I can uphold it.
O Son of the Buddha, from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entire future limit, during that interval, one must not intentionally sell alcohol.
If one commits this offense, it is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva; one loses the Dharma of the forty-two worthy sages. One must not commit it. Can you uphold it?"
"No. (The respondent says: "I can uphold it.
O Son of the Buddha, from this body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entirety of the future, during that interval, one must not speak of the faults of the fourfold assembly.
If one should violate this, it is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva; one loses the dharma of the forty-two worthy sages. One must not violate it. Can you?"
"Will you uphold it? [He] answers, "I can uphold it.
"Son of the Buddha, from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entirety of the future, during that interval, you must not praise yourself or disparage others.
If you should violate this, it is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva; you will lose the Dharma of the forty-two worthy sages. You must not violate it. Can you?"
"Will you uphold it? [He] replies, "I can uphold it.

"Son of the Buddha, from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entirety of the future limit, during that interval, you must not be stingy or harbor malice toward it.
If you should violate this, it is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva; you will lose the Dharma of the forty-two worthy sages. You must not violate it. Can you?"
"Will you uphold it? (He answers: "I can uphold it.
"O Son of the Buddha, from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the entire future limit, during that interval, you must not harbor anger nor refuse repentance.
If there is an offense, it is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva; one loses the Dharma of the forty-two worthy sages. You must not commit an offense."
"Can you uphold this? [He] answers, "I can uphold it.
"Son of the Buddha, from this present body until the attainment of Buddhahood, throughout the entire extent of the future, in the interval between these times, you must not slander the Triple Gem.
If you should violate this, it is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva; you will lose the Dharma of the forty-two worthy sages. You must not violate it. Can you uphold it?"
"No. (He replies: "I can uphold them.
Thus far, the ten grave precepts have been briefly proclaimed. Hereafter, the ritual for the altar will be separately established; you should request instruction from the Ācārya.
You must now recite with a sincere mind and in detail the characteristics of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts within the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. Regarding...
This mind-ground is both perfectly integrated and sequentially arranged; nature and characteristics proceed together. Do not allow them to leak away;
each of you should practice in accordance with these instructions. (The response: “We shall practice in accordance with the instructions” (said three times, answered three times).
The two junior *ācāryas* first recite the ten major precepts in their entirety at the lower altar; the forty-eight minor precepts are recited on the following day.

If, however, the time is long and [the assembly] cannot endure it, they shall descend from their seats after performing the practice according to the instructions, and on the following day, they shall recite the entire text of the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
Chapter Twenty: The Method for Holding the Śikya Staff. Quoting the Invocation, the Eulogy, and the Section on the Essential Distinctions of Wisdom.
The elephant symbolizes perfect penetration; majestic and solitary, it reveals the ancestral style of the Buddha. The holy staff is as lively as a dragon.
Opening and closing, traversing horizontally and vertically, he held up and displayed the lineage of the Patriarchs.

Upon hearing the sound of the chime, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmacakra-pravartaka and all the sons of the Buddhas prostrated three times, then knelt together on their right knees with palms joined.
Invoking the request and making the formal announcement:

the wondrous Way is empty and perfect; it is not represented by forms and is thus difficult to demonstrate. The True Doctrine is profound and remote; it relies upon guidance to provide a path for following.
If one wishes to clarify the Dharma-vehicle of the World-Honored One’s single great matter, one must receive the staff of wisdom of the Tathāgata’s supreme merits.

If one does not seek the true *upadeśa*, how can one awaken to the principles of upholding [the Dharma]? I now request the Master of the [Name] School from [Name] Temple to serve as your *ācārya* and *prajñādanda-upādhyāya* (wisdom-staff preceptor) to provide you with guidance.
As for the words of this request, it is fitting that you state them yourself; however, fearing that you may be unable to do so, I shall speak them on your behalf.
[At this point, recite the Sanskrit verses.]
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, [Name], disciple, seek to enter the Dharma that serves as the ladder and steps for attaining the Way.
I pray that the Virtuous One will act as my instructor and bestow upon me the staff of the Way. Relying upon the Virtuous One, I shall uphold the true wisdom-staff of the Wheel of Dharma.
Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of compassion (one prostration). Out of great compassion (one prostration)."
The Preceptor struck the sounding-block and said:
"O sons of the Buddha, since you have so earnestly extended this invitation, I shall act as your 'Preceptor who Develops the Staff of Wisdom.
You must listen attentively to all my instructions."
It is said that the transmission between the thousand Buddhas, which is the Way of "sealing mind with mind," consists of nothing more than mind and Dharma.
Now, mind cannot be pointed out to others, and Dharma cannot be bestowed upon others. Mind must be awakened; Dharma must be attained. Mind is not a mind that exists as a thing.
If one were to show mind to others, then mind would belong to the realm of existence (*saṃskṛta*). Dharma is fundamentally without-dharma. If one were to [show] Dharma...

When transmitted to others, the Dharma likewise becomes contingent upon existence. If the mental factors (citta-dharma) exist [independently], one is identical to ordinary beings and cannot attain liberation;

if the mental factors do not exist, one falls into the state of a sage and lacks their functional efficacy. Therefore, know that while the person resides in the disciple, the Dharma resides in the teacher.
The mind is like a grain seed; the Dharma is like rain and dew. A person must awaken for themselves; the teacher transmits through the Dharma.

If one does not awaken to their own mind yet attempts to transmit the Way, it is like plowing and sowing without seeds. Conversely, though one may have awakened to the Way for oneself, if one lacks the Dharma, it will ultimately result in sprouting seeds that grow into weeds and filth.
Therefore, the conditions of teacher and disciple must coincide, so that the internal and external may mutually complete one another.

The Master should point out your mind; you should investigate and clarify the principle within yourself. To understand the principle while remaining ignorant of the Dharma is to possess a discriminatory intellect;
when such a mind moves, it becomes inverted, losing the fundamentally luminous Dharma and failing to awaken to the ultimate realization of the mind.
This is surely a false and floating mind. Therefore, to awaken to the true mind, one must realize that the Dharma belongs to the True Master. Thus, our Buddha...
Hei-shi reveals the Dharma-gate of Chan meditation. He desires that all bhikṣus investigate it from time to time, so that both their own minds and the Dharma may be realized.
Therefore, he exhorts them to constantly carry the *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) as they practice, seeking a single moment of awakening.

This staff is the manifestation of the wisdom of one's fundamental mind; through it, the wisdom of the lineage masters is fully integrated at once. Thus it is said: "The *khakkhara* is the staff of wisdom."
Awakening to one's original mind is the virtue of the mind; awakening to the Master’s Dharma is the virtue of its function. Therefore, it is also called the "Virtue Staff" (*de-zhang*).
It causes people to awaken to the distinction between the two wisdoms and to practice the merit of the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle.
This is because, among the five elements of the world, gold is supreme; and among the five metals, tin is the most supple, the whitest, and the most... [resilient].
"Clearness" (*míng*) signifies the clarity, purity, gentleness, and dignity of the mind-ground; thus, the staff is made of clear metal.
Therefore, it is called "light," "clear," "non-retrogressive," "awakened," "unsluggish," "sparse," "gathering," and "accomplishment.
It causes people to lighten their afflictions, clarify their wisdom, transcend the triple world without turning back, awaken suddenly to the True Dharma, and sever their delusions.
It vexes pride and binds one with the fetters of greed and delusion; yet by gathering up precept, concentration, and wisdom, it brings about the fruit of the Buddha-way.

One who can hold this staff should seek and inquire from time to time, so that all wisdom—the worldly and world-transcending teachings heard through much learning—will be clearly understood. All six perfections and ten thousand practices are cultivated toward this end.

As the attendant held up the mendicant’s staff, the Master (the Abbot) took up the staff and showed it, saying: "Do you see it? Do you see it? (Upon hearing [the sound of] the shaking [of the staff]...)
Xuanze said: "Do you hear? Do you hear? (After a long pause, he said: "If you see with the seeing, Xuanze, that seeing is not true seeing.
If you hear with the hearing, Xuanze, that hearing is not true hearing. You must set aside seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to receive it;

only then will the monk’s staff be attained. (He struck the staff once and said: "Do you understand? (After a long pause, he passed the staff to his attendant and said: "If you can understand at this point, then this is the staff in its entirety."
Severing the path between the holy and the ordinary, he has followed a distinct route throughout his life, upholding it day and night.
Because he practices even beyond the realm of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara, and even further beyond that, Magu arrived at Zhangjing carrying his staff.

He circled the meditation seat three times, shook the staff once, and stood there with solemn composure. Zhangjing said, "Right! Right! Magu then went to Nanquan and likewise circled the meditation seat.
He circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his monk’s staff once, and stood there upright. Nanquan said, "Not so, not so.
When Yongjia reached the Sixth Patriarch, he likewise circumambulated the meditation seat, struck his monk’s staff once, and stood there. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. Good son."
If you can realize this matter, it will be well. It is like Chan Master Chou’s flying staff, which resolved a tiger fight;
or like Deng Yinpeng’s flying staff, which resolved a military conflict. These were all instances of upholding the supreme matter of the Patriarchs’ Chan, thereby attaining great mastery.
Now, as for the Patriarchs’ Chan: the Dharmakāya Buddha, being without body and without mouth, directly...
This demonstrates the Dharma of the Mind-essence (citta-garbha). This is what is called the Patriarch of the Buddhas.

If one wishes to bring forth this Dharma that is neither body nor speech, it can only be shown by means of the Reward-Buddha (saṃbhoga-kāya) and the Transformation-Buddha (nirmāṇa-kāya) emitting light and holding up a flower.
As for the Transformation-Buddha indicating it through the faculty of sound and the tongue-wheel, it is beyond the reach of verbal expression. Therefore...
Śākyamuni displayed the *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) to cause people to awaken to the natural splendor of their own original ground; thus it is said, "The Buddha-dharma is not many things.
If you wish to seek the wisdom of differentiation from the place of the transformation Buddha, I shall now, according to the teaching, provide a detailed exposition for all you sons of the Buddha.
This complete staff is the wondrous path of the Supreme Vehicle. This is what our Buddha [has transmitted] from...

This refers to the fact that beginning with the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka* and culminating in the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, these encompass the entire body of temporal teachings throughout his lifetime.
At the center of this staff, a tube is first erected vertically; above the tube there are five protrusions, and while the interior of the tube is empty, its exterior is solid.

This demonstrates the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which—through the interplay of emptiness and the conventional (*śūnyatā* and *saṃvṛti*)—transcends the four logical extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*) and fully realizes them.
The True Dharma is its foundation. Its five prongs above symbolize the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*).

Flanking them with two prongs symbolizes the Two Truths. These two pairs represent the Four Noble Truths. The six rings on the two prongs represent the practice of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

These six pairs represent the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Below, the three bells represent the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) as well as the [three trainings of] precept, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*).
It represents the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. It is the supreme crown, the mark of the invisible crown. It is the ultimate limit of the Dharma.

Therefore, the sixteen [spokes] represent the practice of the Four Noble Truths (suffering, origin, cessation, and path), the Four Immeasurables (loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity), the Four Dhyānas, and the Four Formless Attainments.

The three tiers and four prongs combined make seven; these represent the Seven Factors of Enlightenment and the Seven Noble Riches. Including the bell and the drill, there are eight, representing the Eight Liberations.
Thus, there is nothing among the categories of all dharmas—such as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three insights, and the eight liberations—that is not fully contained herein.
This is the supramundane dharma of the Three Vehicles across the five periods. As for mundane dharmas, they are forged into the vajra-wheel.
The upper part represents the summit of Mount Sumeru; the entire staff represents a single world-system. The middle section represents the root of non-arising ignorance.
The two-pronged [vajra] represents the two dharmas of existence and non-existence. The three-pronged [vajra] represents the suffering of the three miserable realms.

The four-pronged [vajra] represents birth, old age, sickness, and death. The five protrusions represent the afflictions of the five destinies. The six rings represent the six realms of existence. As for the seventh...

The seven destinies and the eight difficulties constitute the phenomena of this world. This staff must not be allowed to touch the ground, signifying that one must not cling to either worldly or world-transcending phenomena.
"Day and night following" means they must not be separated; one must not depart from the True Dharma of the world.
One should constantly hold it so as not to lose it, shaking its sound to reach the faculty of hearing and bring about realization.
This is the supreme and perfect penetration (*parama-parama pariccheda*). One must constantly wipe it clean so that no dust or grime accumulates;

this means that the ground of the mind (*citta-bhūmi*) must not be obscured, and the Wheel of Dharma (*dharma-cakra*) must not fail to turn. This encompasses both the teachings for humans and devas and the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), yet it refers specifically to the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
A *bhikṣu* must not remain ignorant of or fail to realize this. Regarding the method of holding the staff (*daṇḍa*), there are twenty-five matters; first, by...

The ten matters are as follows: seeing the staff and hearing the staff, yet not harming the insects in the earth; holding the staff so that the elderly may rely upon it; holding it specifically for the purpose of almsround (*piṇḍapāta*);

one must not move it forward or backward, nor carry it on the shoulder, nor hold it horizontally; upon seeing the Buddha, one must not make a sound; when entering among the assembly, one must not be arrogant;
raising and holding the venerable *khakkhara* (monk's staff); one must not lean the staff against the back of a house; this is the proper way.
One must not go out with a staff after midday. Regarding those who wish to go out with a staff after midday:

it is permissible for one who has been invited from afar, one visiting a sick person, one escorting a deceased person, or one invited by non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) for the four requisites. One must not draw on the ground with a staff. Three teachers may not all go out with staffs simultaneously.
One must not carry a staff while traveling together with four people, except for the Elder (sthavira). One must not carry [a staff] universally [in all cases].

Upon arriving at the gate of a donor's house, one should enter with proper deportment. First, shake out [the robe] three times; if no one comes out after shaking it three times, proceed to another house of a donor.
When exiting, one should carry the staff, holding it in the center of the left hand. The staff should always remain in one’s own room and not be separated from the body.
Its lower end must not touch the ground so as not to cause the cloth to soil; it must be polished and wiped clean every day. Regarding the staff:
When intending to go out, one must receive [the bell] from a śrāmaṇera; if there is no śrāmaṇera, even a layperson may do so.
While holding it, carry it with heaven above and earth below, placing it beneath the armpit and gripping it with the little finger, ensuring both ends are level and not uneven.
When it rings, let it ring constantly; when silent, let it remain soundless. When it rings, let the sound be even and subtle, maintaining this harmony at all times. If it is the first *saṃgha*...

The monk places the staff on his left foot, while the nun places hers on her right foot as they enter the house of a donor (*dānapati*). They should visit no more than three houses nearby or seven houses at the furthest distance;

they must not travel further than this. Within these limits, they may receive food. When placing the staff, it should be suspended from a tree, or laid across the ground, or used for sleeping upon a stone;

in such cases, the staff should lie aligned with the body. When placed inside a bed, it should be positioned so that it is level with the body. While traveling on the road, the head of the staff should always point forward.
The staff is the Buddha’s body; because the myriad practices reside within it. If it were to lean or tilt, the myriad things would find no peace;

if it remains level and upright, the myriad things attain their proper place. When the base of the stand touches the ground, the intense sufferings of the three miserable realms (trāya) are constantly suspended in the air, thereby uprooting the calamities of the three realms.
This staff is that which has been transmitted among all Buddhas; when a bhikṣu holds it, it serves as the emblem of the ladder for entering the Path.
Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha: if you wish for great awakening, you should first investigate the Ancestral Teacher’s Chan at all times.
If you wish to clarify the Dharma, you should next minutely examine the Tathāgata’s Chan. The staff is precisely the one mind; the staff is precisely the Buddha; the staff is precisely the Dharma;
the staff is precisely ordinary beings and sages; the staff is precisely the various conditions of form and mind; the staff is precisely the One.
All matters are ultimately firm and solid. You should always hold this staff; always polish it and always sweep it; always keep it in mind and always attend to it.
Thus, immeasurable Dharma gates and hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings will be fully perfected at once.

You should give rise to the heart to extensively deliver sentient beings and make the vow to equally attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Such practice and maintenance possess unsurpassed merit; therefore, it is called "Wisdom."

The staff is the virtue of the staff; it is the direct cause and direct fruit of generating the bodhicitta. Since you are able to receive and uphold it, you should practice in accordance with the instructions.

(The Preceptor holds the staff, shakes it three times, recites the verse and mantra, and transmits it one by one. The bhikṣu stands up and receives the staff, reciting the verse: [Verse for Receiving the Staff]
Yongjia often said: "The tiger's staff with its two-pronged prongs, its golden rings jingling clearly—this is not a mere display of form in vain;
it is the personal trace of one who personally wields the Tathāgata’s precious staff."
The mantra is recited as follows: Oṃ kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛtāntapate naya bhañja hūṃ phaṭ (three times).
The verse says:
Holding the *khakkhara* staff, I vow that all sentient beings May establish great assemblies of giving And reveal the path of suchness.

(The *Upādhyāya* bows to the Buddha and returns to his quarters. The *bhikṣu* holding the staff walks ahead, escorting him to the front of the quarters. He waits for the *Upādhyāya* to enter, then returns to the hall to hang up the staff. Afterwards, assuming the full dignified demeanor, he enters the quarters to offer thanks.)
Chapter Twenty-Four: Distinguishing the Bestowal of Precepts.
Whenever one first receives the precepts, one must first take refuge in the Triple Gem. Once one has taken refuge in the Triple Gem, the essence of the precepts is already complete.
Why is this? It is because taking refuge in the Buddha is to possess one’s own mind; one’s own mind is the Dharmakāya. Taking refuge in the Dharma is to possess the radiance of one’s own mind;
that radiance is the Saṃbhogakāya. Taking refuge in the Saṅgha is to possess the purity of one’s own mind.
The pure one is the nirmāṇakāya. The threefold refuge—namely, the dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and nirmāṇakāya—is entirely present within one's own mind.
The pure one is the nirmāṇakāya. The threefold refuge—namely, the dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and nirmāṇakāya—is entirely present within one's own mind.
When one's own mind has no precepts to receive, it fully encompasses all precepts, both great and small.

When the radiance of one's own mind does not depend upon the performance of good deeds, it fully encompasses all wholesome dharmas, both great and small. When one's own mind is pure, it does not require further precepts;
it naturally benefits both oneself and others—this is the Threefold Pure Precept (Tri-śikṣā-saṃvara). The Buddha is the Dharma-body (Dharmakāya).
The Dharma is *prajñā*; the Saṃgha is liberation (*vimukti*). The Dharma-body possesses both *prajñā* and liberation;

*prajñā* possesses liberation and the Dharma-body; liberation possesses the Dharma-body and *prajñā*. Like characters linked in a continuous chain, none may be missing, for all must return [to the source].
This returning employs the "three threes," yet the three and one return as one. The three returns and three knots signify the accomplishment of the Dharma. Once this single Dharma is...
The great task is now accomplished. What more need be said of sin? What more need be said of precepts? What more need be said of discipline?

And what more need be said of cultivation and realization? Therefore, it is called the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-tattva*). Yet, fearing that the ordinary mind has not yet attained clarity and that the phenomenal aspects have not yet reached perfection, one further demonstrates the method of repentance through the ritual of *karmavācanā*.
This ritual of repentance is to be held in profound reverence. As for the essence, there is nothing too great or too small; as for the Way, it exists...
Regarding the differences in rank: first, the general characteristics of the precepts are shown. In the Great Text, there are five [categories]:

the five abandonments of the ten evils, the five productions of the ten virtues, and the five endowments of the five constants. These constitute the mental conduct of humans and devas. Once one knows that the essence of the precepts exists, it is the Buddha’s precept;
this is what is common to both monastics and laypeople alike. However, while the laity possess the desires of husband and wife, the monastics have none at all.

The ear is purified. The Three Refuges constitute the substance; the Five Precepts serve as the protection. For one who receives the precepts, it is the receiving of the substance and the application of the protection;

it is not the acceptance of the five types of penal names. These precepts are the root. As for leaving the household life and shaving the head, one must further understand what distinguishes this [from the lay precepts].
Why? Because the Buddha possesses but a single mind and has never categorized [his followers]; yet, as there are superior and inferior levels of the Way, he manifested progressive stages.
Therefore, in worldly convention, humans and devas are ranked together, while the Sangha selects those of the Buddha-seed; thus, there is a distinction between the refined and the mixed.

It can be seen that being a monk is truly the business of a great man (mahāpuruṣa), something that neither generals nor ministers can achieve. Consequently, when one intends to leave the household life, the Buddha established a rule to first inquire about the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*).
The first is to ask whether one relies on rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*) rather than soft, warm garments; one who does not so rely may not join the Sangha.
First, those who rely on the practice of alms-gathering but instead habitually consume food provided by families are not to be included in the ranks of the Sangha.
Second, those who rely on sitting under trees but instead dwell in houses and buildings according to their preference for shelter are not to be included in the ranks of the Sangha.

Third, those who rely on medicinal decoctions of decayed substances but instead habitually consume sweet and smooth delicacies are not to be included in the ranks of the Sangha. Those who may be permitted are [those who] achieve greatness.
After the Sangha has been established, if one is ill or aged, it is merely for the sake of expediency that this is said.

Once the four reliances have been established, one next inquires whether there are prohibitions regarding parents, prohibitions regarding kings or officials, or prohibitions regarding creditors; if indeed there are no such prohibitions, one should then examine the candidate’s faculties.
Only when they are not a vessel ruined by the seven obstacles, not of a lineage deluded by external paths, and not someone who owes debts to others, is it appropriate [to proceed].

The procedure for the middle-ranking monk is indeed according to the ritual. Only then does one shave his hair. On the day of the tonsure and ordination, he is further instructed in repentance and further instructed in taking refuge.
One pours water upon the crown of his head and severs the karmic knots at the crown, demonstrating to him the matters concerning the Buddha’s uṣṇīṣa;

this is the conferral of the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*). Once the essence is fully established, one then demonstrates the characteristics of the ten precepts. The five precepts are the same as before. [End of] Old [Record].
This is the essential character of a śrāmaṇera. Regarding the five precepts that follow, the prohibition against greed is paramount. In body, one must not crave ornamental finery;
in speech, hearing, sight, and physical action, one must not crave amusement or pleasure; one must not crave high or superior seats and bedding; one must not crave more than a single meal;
and one must not crave the enjoyment of gold and jewels. For a śrāmaṇera is the seed of the great Saṃgha; he ought to be exclusively diligent and pure.

Regarding the great beneficial activity for oneself and others before one has yet begun it, there is a fear that one’s own affairs may become difficult to advance, and conversely turn into obstacles to the Way.

Once one has become a *śrāmaṇera*, one is already solemnly like a *bhikṣu*. Therefore, by serving the *bhikṣus* and exhausting one’s own personal practice, one is further able to observe the conduct of the Great Beings.
When such practice has continued for a long time, the minor training (*kṣudra-śikṣā*) is perfected; as for age—
Having reached twenty years of age and being verified as a true man, one then selects the foundation for a bhikṣu.

As for the foundation of a bhikṣu, one selects those whose faculties and talents are those of a genuine great man (mahāpuruṣa), who are free from any of the obstacles or disqualifications, and who are persons capable of upholding the True Dharma.
Whenever a śrāmaṇera is about to receive the full precepts, he first gathers virtuous elders (bhadanta) from the ten directions whose names and reputations correspond to their actual qualities.

Ten monks constitute the ten masters (*daśācārya*), which is the very seat of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Having selected a pure site, one first establishes the altar ritual according to the Dharma.
The ten masters each occupy their respective quarters. When the time for the conferral of the precepts has been set, prior to ascending the altar:
The Upādhyāya first dispatched the Ācārya to interrogate the śrāmaṇera one by one in a secluded place.

Only when it was determined that the śrāmaṇera was free from the thirteen grave obstacles (*gurudharma*) and the sixteen minor impediments (*mṛdu-pratibandha*) would he be permitted to ascend the altar. Regarding what are called the thirteen grave obstacles:
the śrāmaṇera must first answer the teacher with a straightforward mind. First, after receiving the five precepts and the śrāmaṇera precepts, he must not have committed any transgression.
The four pārājika offenses: First, having received the precepts, not to commit killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or lying;
if one commits any of these four, one is a person on the shore of the ocean of the Buddha-dharma. Second, not to violate a pure bhikṣuṇī, thereby destroying both one's own and her precepts.

Third, "living as a thief" (caura-vāsa), which means when one was a śrāmaṇera, one eavesdropped while the great saṃgha recited the precepts and falsely assumed the status of a bhikṣu to participate in the formal legal procedures (karmavācanā) of the great saṃgha.

Fourth, those who have violated both the inner and outer paths: this refers to those who were formerly followers of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), who having abandoned error and returned to the right path, received the Buddha’s precepts and became followers of the inner path;
yet they subsequently violated the inner path by performing the deeds of non-Buddhists, and now have returned once more to the inner path.
Because they have entered and exited both the inner and outer paths, thereby violating both ways, they are excluded. Fifth, eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*). As for eunuchs:
The "one who is not a male by birth" refers to one born without the male organ. The "castrated non-male" refers to one whose male organ has been removed with a blade.
The "jealous non-male" refers to one who originally lacks a male organ but suddenly develops one upon seeing others engaged in sexual intercourse, giving rise to feelings of jealous desire.

The "transformed non-male" refers to one who sees a man turn into a woman or a woman turn into a man. The "partial non-male" refers to one who is a man for half the month and [a woman for the other half].
Those who take women as their wives are all vessels of impurity, moved by the karma of lust; they do not possess the marks of a bhikṣu. Sixth, killing one’s father;
seventh, killing one’s mother—these are grave acts of unfiliality that violate the sanctity of the living body. Eighth, killing an arhat—this harms one who has attained the fruit of the path.
Ninth, breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha—that is, disrupting the *karmavācanā* and the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. These are great [offenses].

10. Causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by inciting strife and breaking up the community, thereby obstructing the performance of the *dharmakarma* and severing the life-force of the Buddha-lineage.
11. Shedding the blood of a Buddha, because of inflicting injury upon the Buddha. 12. Non-humans (*amanuṣya*), because devas, ghosts, and spirits do not possess the physical body of a bhikṣu.
13. Animals (*tiryagyoni*), because nāgas, beasts, and demons employ transformations, illusions, and deceit. 14. [The fourteenth...]
These two types of hermaphrodites possess both male and female organs; because their sexual organs are wondrously licentious and strange, they constitute these thirteen [excluded categories].
They greatly deviate from the True Dharma, and the Dharma does not permit them to become bhikṣus. Therefore, when the Buddha saves those who bear the Dharma, he values the bhikṣu most highly.

A bhikṣu is a true teacher of humanity and heaven; he must not be borrowed from or mixed with such [unqualified persons]. If one has not yet reached the highest level and attained great penetration and great awakening, [one must remain as a lay follower].
Next, one perceives that the nature of sin is empty; subsequently, one performs repentance with bitter earnestness. One may perceive light, flowers, and various auspicious omens.
Those who enter as Bodhisattvas are not of the Buddha-seed; they lack these grave obstacles and have already fulfilled the essential requirements.
Furthermore, one must inquire regarding the sixteen minor impediments (*mṛdu-pratibandha*): first, one must know one’s own name; second, one must know the name of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
First, there is a reason for the transmission of the Dharma from teacher to disciple. Second, one must be twenty years of age, so as not to treat it as mere play.

Third, the robes, fourth, the alms bowl, and fifth, the bedding and requisites—these three must be complete, so as to accord with the Buddha-dharma. Sixth, one must have the permission of one's parents, so as to avoid opposition.
Seventh, one must not be burdened by debts to others, so as to be free from worldly entanglements. Eighth, one must not be a non-human being.

10. One who is not a servant or messenger, because his person is not bound by low status; 11. One who is not an official or minister of the current court, because he does not contravene royal decrees;
12. One who is already twenty years of age, capable of enduring cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, observing the precepts of eating once a day, and patiently enduring harsh words.
One who endures venomous insects is called a "great man" (*mahāpuruṣa*), for he is capable of practicing the Dharma. Twelfth, those with leprosy;
thirteenth, carbuncles; fourteenth, white leprosy; fifteenth, consumption; sixteenth, insanity—none of these possess the marks of a great man.

Therefore, only after one has carefully examined that there are no such prohibitions or obstacles will the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion and three-fold proclamation) be permitted, and the method for conferring the status of a bhikṣu be granted. Indeed...
The Buddha established the Dharma for bhikṣus as follows: one must select only those whose *śīla-ātmabhāva* (precept-body) and human character are exemplary.

When the *śīla-ātmabhāva* is pure and white and the human character is fully endowed, this is called being "fully possessed of the precepts" (*upasaṃpanna*). To understand the *śīla-ātmabhāva*, it is sufficient to possess a sincere mind:

that there be no "heavy obstacles" (*gurudharmāntarāya*) that hinder the mind, and no "light hindrances" (*laghvantarāya*) that hinder the body. With both body and mind pure, the ten masters grant their permission and perform the formal ritual of *karmavācanā*.

Having been polished [by the precepts], one immediately enters the rank of a bhikṣu. Regarding the ten masters: first is the Upādhyāya, the Dharma-lord who acts on behalf of the Buddha to propagate the teachings;
second is the Karmācārya; third is the Śikṣācārya; and the fourth through the tenth are the Sākṣin-ācāryas (witnessing masters).
When about to ascend the altar, two persons lead the way while sounding the chime, guiding the śrāmaṇeras.
Arriving at the quarters of the ten masters, he performs three prostrations before each. He invites the ten masters to the Dharma Hall, where they take their seats in a single row.
He leads the procession to draw the name-slips of the ten masters, pointing them out one by one with clarity.

Next, leading the śrāmaṇeras, he makes the formal announcement (vācanā), requesting that such-and-such a Venerable serve as the Upādhyāya for the conferral of precepts, such-and-such a Venerable as the Karmācārya, and such-and-such a Venerable...
The Preceptor for Instruction (ācārya-śikṣācārya) and the Venerable One who serves as the Preceptor for Authorization (ācārya-jñapticārya) each grant their consent.

Thereafter, having ascended the altar, circumambulated it, and completed the ritual prostrations, they offer prayers for the Emperor and praises to the Buddha. Once seated, when the time for questioning arrives, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) is performed.
The Upādhyāya asks: "Who will act as the Karman-master (karman-ācārya) for these śrāmaṇeras? When the Karman is approved, he further asks: "Who [will perform the Karman]?"
He acts as the preceptor for the śrāmaṇeras. Once the instruction is approved, he is appointed as the preceptor. He steps out from the assembly and performs the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion).

Having been formally appointed as the preceptor, he conducts the instruction and leads the various disciples down from the platform. In a place where the nine masters can see him but cannot hear him, he questions each one individually regarding the obstacles and impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*).
Since these śrāmaṇeras have already been previously vetted, they all respond, saying: [They answer "no" to each question].

"No. Then, he is summoned again into the great assembly. Facing the assembly, the *jñapti* (formal motion) is recited. Once the *jñapti* has been completed, the witness-teacher (*sākṣin*) should grant his assent, provided there are no obstacles or impediments.

Thereafter, the *karmācārya* (preceptor of rituals) inspires the highest measure of resolve, causing him to vow to sever all evil, vow to cultivate all goodness, and vow to deliver all sentient beings, rather than seeking the minor fruits of a *śrāvaka*, but desiring directly to achieve [Buddhahood].
Regarding the Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), one should correctly seek to give rise to the "aspiration for enlightenment" (*bodhicitta*).

As for this "aspiration for enlightenment," it refers to the mind that sets out to practice *chan* meditation, to awaken to the Unsurpassed Way, and to attain Buddhahood in order to deliver sentient beings. Because this has not yet reached true awakening, it is merely called the "aspiration for enlightenment" and is not yet termed "Bodhicitta.
Once the aspiration for enlightenment has been generated, one is then capable of shouldering the True Dharma; therefore, the Buddha established the rite for bestowing the *śrāmaṇera* precepts.

The reason for the *bhikṣu* precepts is to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time. If one were to give rise to the narrow mind of a *śrāvaka*, the True Dharma would perish and no one would be able to bear its burden.
The *bhikṣu* precepts are called the *śrāvaka* precepts; through the ritual of the fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), one attains a pure body and performs the conduct of a *śrāvaka*.
By exerting oneself upon this pure body to arouse the resolve, one stimulates the superior mind that is the seed of the Buddha. Only then does one [truly]...
The *karmavācanā* is performed three times so that the ritual may be accomplished; this constitutes the completion of the attainment of the precepts.

Nowadays, people do not recognize what constitutes the Buddha’s precepts, mistakenly identifying them as the four *pārājika*, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the two *aniyata*, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the ninety *pāyattika*, and the four *prātideśanīya*.

The one hundred rules of training for *bhikṣuṇīs* constitute the *bhikṣu* precepts. Consequently, upon the ordination platform, rather than employing the ten masters, one uses only the ritual invitation.
One proclaims: "Regarding the four *pārājika* dharmas, are you able to uphold them? [The candidate] replies: "I am able to uphold them. [The officiant] thinks to himself:
"These four *pārājikas* are the most heinous and grave offenses. What transgression have I committed that I should receive and uphold them? As for the names of the remaining precepts...
Indeed. Why such excessive self-abasement? It is because these two hundred and fifty offenses, both light and grave, were established during the Buddha’s lifetime.
As the bhikṣus gradually violated their pure precepts, the Buddha prescribed punishments according to the gravity of the offense so that people would refrain from transgressing them.
Therefore, it is called the characteristic of precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*). Now, as for the multiplicity of these characteristics, how could they be limited to only two hundred and fifty?

This is merely an enumeration of the major outlines of transgressions committed by people of the past, intended to enable later generations to infer and avoid them accordingly. If a person can constantly maintain a pure and pristine body, [they will be free from such faults].

Those whose resolve for the supreme path is of the highest grade naturally do not fall into this category; how could they be considered those for whom formal legal statutes were first established to be upheld?
Since the Buddha formulated the precepts, they have been called the *vinaya*, which refers to the detailed classification and meticulous analysis that prevents confusion or intermingling.
Therefore, after the conferral of the precepts, a specific instructor is appointed to guide them, distinguishing them from those who are merely new students.
The Master [Kāśyapa] recited the characteristics of the precepts in detail, first expounding the four *pārājika* rules; this is called "according to their characteristics" (*anuloma*).

This was because monks, having already received the precepts, did not know how to maintain them in purity; since they were unaware of what constituted an offense, they would commit grave transgressions.

The Buddha instructed that in the future, after the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) has been performed, one must first explain these four *pārājika* dharmas to them. The same applies to the remaining categories.
One should know this: having already become a bhikṣu and passed many years of seniority (*vassa*), with that seniority complete and the virtue of the mind perfected, one realizes the Great Way.
Only after truly giving rise to the *bodhicitta* does one enter the stage of *bodhi*, being called a *bodhisattva*.
If a bhikṣu cannot attain initial awakening, he must nevertheless investigate the Great Matter; this is precisely the stage of the bodhisattva’s causal ground.
Thus, in the Brahmajāla Sūtra, the Reward Body Buddha preached the Mind-Ground Precepts and emitted a single ray of light from his mouth, which was then emitted from the mouth of Śākyamuni.
Light. However, if one can understand the Dharma taught by this light, it is called "understanding the words of the Dharma Master.
Regardless of whether they are humans, devas, animals, ghosts, male or female practitioners of lust, or others, all may receive the precepts.
If one does not recognize this, one does not understand the words of the Dharma Master and should not receive the precepts; this can be known thereby. If one recognizes this light, one attains all...

The Buddha’s Mind-Seal is precisely this single lineage that came from the West. Once one has attained this lineage, the ten grave offenses and forty-eight light transgressions will certainly not be committed.
Nowadays, people do not recognize the ground of the mind; they merely see "dry radish-head Chan" proceeding in a state of constant confusion.

Consequently, there are practitioners of Chan who violate even a single precept, making it difficult for others to believe them. Furthermore, there are those who, failing to recognize the ground of the mind, act recklessly...

The four white [teachings] culminate in the ground of the final mind, where one finally beholds the Buddha’s original intent. This does not exceed the goal of causing the Dharma to abide long;
a single phrase encompasses it all. It is precisely for this reason that there are distinctions between the prior and the subsequent, the great and the small, and the opening and closing.

Regarding this matter, only Chan can provide a thorough understanding. If one does not engage in Chan practice, then returning to the self is merely returning to the self, and observing the precepts is merely observing the precepts.
The small remains small; the great remains great. The Pure Land remains the Pure Land; the Chan school remains the Chan school.
To wander blindly along every path and divide the river to drink from it is to create the karma of the great hells—this is truly pitiable.

With no other choice, I have ventured to disregard the axes and halberds of various schools and respectfully present this for my fellow disciples. I hope that those of like mind will examine and revise it together. I do not dare [claim originality].
To invent one's own arbitrary theories in order to invite the great sin of slandering the Dharma is unacceptable.

As for the other subtle distinctions within the Vinaya, one should naturally consult extensively with masters who have studied the Vinaya; this is not a matter for those who are ignorant or shortsighted.

Furthermore, I have heard that some people nowadays rely on the national prohibition against opening ordination platforms (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) and consequently claim that the precepts should not be conferred privately. The ritual protocols had long been obscured and eventually fell into total ruin. Alas! Our dynasty’s founding Emperor, following the lineage of successive illustrious reigns, clarified and reaffirmed the monastic precepts.

For instance, on the thirteenth day of the third month in the tenth year of the Hongwu era, Zhang [Yuanlong], Minister of the Court of Ceremonies, and others submitted a memorial at the Fengtian Gate;
