One day, Cui Zhao, the Minister of Rites, and others, in accordance with the Imperial decree, prepared the original text for circulation throughout the empire.

On the sixth day of the second month in the fifth year of the Yongle era, civil and military officials petitioned at the Fengtian Gate, and it was decreed that the Ministry of Rites be instructed to reissue the proclamation and open the period of abstinence.
This is clearly recorded in official documents. How weighty is this law and how venerable these precepts of the State! Hereafter—

In recent times, due to the Northern Precept Platform (Beijietan), eunuchs have established courtesans as "shaven-headed soldiers. This single instance of depravity has been so pervasive that it has corrupted the very essence of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Furthermore, it has led to the wasteful expenditure of state funds; thus, there arose the debate regarding the prohibition and reopening of the precept platforms.

Since the prohibition, veteran masters and long-established virtuous elders have maintained their vows until the end of their lives, withdrawing from public life and ceasing to preach. (The year) was the Yihai of the Wanli era.
Lately, those of later generations who claim to be scholars have not received the precepts themselves, nor have they witnessed the ritual of the altar for the transmission of the Dharma.

They universally maintain that the precepts should not be conferred upon oneself and must wait for the state to lift its prohibitions; consequently, they have relegated the Vinaya-piṭaka to a place of uselessness.

They merely practice the lecturing of sutras to indulge their own opinions, causing later generations and junior students to follow this tradition of valuing the superficial over the essential, openly committing violations of the precepts. Since this is so—
Those who claim to know the mind-ground have fallen into extreme slander; even those who practice Chan have turned away from the True Dharma and spread heterodox teachings at will.

As the True Dharma of the Chan school is on the verge of extinction, this state of affairs has persisted for so long that it has caused those among the "unreliable" outside the four classes of society—who lack the restraint of monastic precepts—to treat shaving the head as a mere repository for filth and evil. Consequently, they do not slightly conform to worldly laws.

Those who are thus accommodated immediately shave their heads themselves and enter the Dharma-gate by force. Since these various unworthy individuals lack the true Dharma, they cannot be driven out through the maintenance of discipline or formal admonition.
Once they have become accustomed to such frivolous excess, even when laypeople see them consuming meat, alcohol, and engaging in sexual impurity, it is no longer considered extraordinary;
consequently, there is no further censure or suspicion. They fall outside the reach of secular law, yet they do not arrive at the realm of the Buddha-Dharma.
No one promotes [the Dharma]. Even if it were promoted, it would instead be treated as an offense; it is prohibited and cast aside.

Hidden away and stolen, they harbor baseless anxieties, fearing that some unforeseen calamity might occur in the future, causing both the Buddha-dharma and the state laws to suffer ruin. This cannot be understood.

For those among the Sangha who possess blood and breath, how could they sit idly by while witnessing the calamity of the Dharma-gate where livers and brains are being smeared upon the ground, without urgently practicing the precepts to discipline the assembly?

However, I fear that because the laws of the precepts have been submerged for so long, if one were suddenly to disregard personal reputation and incur the world’s hatred and resentment to rectify the Buddha's precepts, it would likely be impossible to fully investigate their origins; furthermore—
If there are deficiencies in ritual and dharma, then the censure of deviant discipline may not be avoided. Speaking of this with deep pain, I cannot help but shed tears.
Recently, the late Emperor Shenzong was sagely, wise, and exceptionally gifted; in his later years, he deeply realized that Buddhist precepts are beneficial to the worldly path.

Based on the petition submitted by the monk Yuanqing of Mount Wutai, the Emperor was moved to graciously bestow robes, an alms bowl, a mendicant’s staff, and several thousand strings of cash for vegetarian offerings.
An imperial decree was transmitted through the eunuch Zhang Ran, granting permission to administer the precepts within the mountains.

According to this, how could it be said that the state ever strictly prohibited the transmission of the precepts between masters and disciples in the mountains? As for the current practice at Yunqi of alternating the position of the monastery supervisor—
These individuals were all disciples of the Bodhisattva precepts. It appears that the Great Master Lianchi once personally ascended the seat to preach the Dharma and confer them upon them.

Toward the end of his life, he happened to encounter a karmic condition and temporarily suspended this practice; however, he subsequently established the method for performing the ritual of the ordination platform (*li-tan*) to study the precepts.

Furthermore, as the primary provision of the *Sengyue* (Monastic Code), he emphasized the cultivation of virtuous conduct through the precepts, stating that they should be put into practice and awaiting the opening of a formal ordination platform before proceeding.

Regarding the conferral of the precepts: what is it that is truly held in high esteem? To stubbornly cling to provisional teachings and thereby sever the seeds of the Buddha is a transgression of the utmost gravity.
Be cautious! Be cautious with the precepts!

Chapter Twenty-Five: Advancing in the Precepts and Demonstrating the Words In studying the Buddha, leaving the household life is of primary importance; for those who have become monks, advancing in the precepts is paramount. On the very day of one's initial tonsure and ordination, one receives the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera.

This is analogous to the Confucian tradition, where during childhood one first studies the "Elementary Learning" (xiǎoxué) to learn filial piety toward parents, respect for elders, and conscientious trustworthiness.
Universal love, kindness toward kin, and ritual propriety such as sweeping and responding to others constitute the foundation of the *Great Learning*.
Therefore, a śrāmaṇera restrains evil and guards against transgression by training in dignified deportment (*vīrya*) within the ten precepts;

within the various aspects of practice, he is made to know how to sever the ten evils—such as greed, anger, and delusion—and to cultivate various virtues such as the patience and wisdom that transcend birth and death, while receiving his teachers and elders with proper deference in every movement.

Regarding such matters as bowing and circumambulation, one should become a fundamental seed for the great bhikṣus. Alas, in this degenerate age of the Final Dharma, people are mostly indolent and negligent;
though they receive the ten precepts, they lack true sincerity. These "name-only" śrāmaṇeras despise and abandon the dharma of the precepts, even if they do not actually break them.

There is also no progress; they treat dignified conduct lightly and have no desire for study or instruction. They value worldly affairs and prioritize repentance over the practice and realization of the precepts.
They entrust themselves to idle leisure, studying empty texts and superficial literature, which only serves to increase their sense of self and others.

As long as there is something to be gained in talk, they fear most of all practicing authentically. They merely wish to quickly perfect the Bodhisattva precepts so that they may handle silver coins and pose as great men.
Willingly becoming a bhikṣu, he was only afraid of being bound by physical restraints and minor details.

When discussing these forms, they do not know what constitutes the ten grave offenses (*daśa-guru-āpatti*) or what constitutes the minor defilements (*laghu-mala*).

This is Zen! It is said that one holds a pig’s head in hand while reciting the pure precepts; yet, not knowing the characteristics of the precepts, how could they possibly transcend their substance?

Alas, the degeneration of the Buddha-dharma lies solely in the mind’s lack of respect. One treats the small as major, yet the major is not truly major. Since the major is not true, the small can be understood by extension.
When a śrāmaṇera does not abide in his śrāmaṇera duties, he oversteps his station by imagining himself a bhikṣu or a bodhisattva.
Sā. The bodhisattva does not understand the precepts. Departing from their proper station, they speak of the Way and speak of dhyāna.

Indeed, you are truly a frivolous, petty, and unprincipled monk who leads a hundred other frivolous and unprincipled followers with his reckless chanting.

As for "Mi" (Maitreya), one should respect and read it thoroughly, carefully expounding the *vinaya*. Then, before the teacher, one should prostrate;

On the fifteenth day of the third month, the precepts were formally administered.

Among the novices who had already received the ten precepts for two years and had not committed any grave or minor offenses, their conduct was examined for its merits and faults. It was found that their practice was in perfect accord with the precepts and dignified decorum (*vinaya-ācāra*).

Only those whose mountain-dwelling practices are known by the entire community are truly [qualified].

Even if one was a layperson or a *śrāmaṇera* when one previously committed lust and defiled a pure-practice *bhikṣuṇī*, the offense is extremely grave and does not permit entry into the precepts.

First, one who has previously eavesdropped upon the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) of the great monks and falsely claimed to be a *bhikṣu*, thereby receiving offerings and prostrations from others, is called a "thief-dweller" (*caura-vāsin*).

Second, one who has never undergone the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of fourfold motion), yet once at some location received three types of robes (*trikaṭuka-cīvara*) and consequently considers himself to have received the full precepts, is termed a "mistakenly recognized *bhikṣu*. He must undergo repentance and receive [the precepts] again.
Regarding the *śukla-jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of a white motion followed by three proclamations) for the precepts:

there are those from non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*), such as the five divisions and six volumes of the "Mysterious Gate" (*xuanmen*) or the Catholic Church, who have already renounced their former ways to receive the Buddhist precepts, yet later revert to practicing non-Buddhist paths and continue to associate with such outsiders.

If they return once more to receive the precepts, this indicates an unstable disposition; such individuals are called "those who break both internal and external [discipline]" and do not belong to the Buddha-dharma.

Vessels [of the Dharma]: The Buddha did not permit the ordination of five kinds of *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs/impotent persons). The Buddha did not permit the ordination of those who have shed the blood of a Buddha;

those who have murdered their father, murdered their mother, murdered their *upādhyāya*, murdered their *ācārya*, disrupted the *saṃgha* that is performing the *karmavācanā* for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, or murdered an *arhat*.

These are called the seven grave offenses (*ānantarya-karma*). The Buddha did not permit their ordination. Furthermore, he did not permit the ordination of those who slander *chan* meditation or slander the Pure Land.

They slander the upholding of the precepts and advocate for "Chan meditation" (Zen), claiming that no one has attained further realization since recent times and that only the ancients could achieve it.
Furthermore, they say that the principles of the Daoist teachings are identical to the principles of Chan, so there is no need for arduous investigation; why not simply study the scriptures?

They advocate for reciting the Buddha’s name, asserting that the principle of "single-mindedness without distraction" can never be realized, and that only the ancients could achieve it. They merely urge people to continue reciting in this manner and speak of the transmission and reception of the precepts.

Such a person is said to have violated the national prohibitions and is not permitted to receive the precepts; they need only recite the Buddha’s name. Furthermore, it is said that upholding the precepts requires only that one does not part from one's robes and bowl;
there is no need to engage in Zen meditation to seek awakening regarding the essence of the precepts. In this Age of Semblance Dharma, one must not take things too seriously.
One should simply act according to the occasion. Do not practice Chan; do not seek the Pure Land; do not receive the precepts. Just shave your head and that is it.
This is precisely what a person who has committed the five heinous crimes does.
The sons of gods and the asuras are called "non-humans" (*amanuṣya*); if they transform into human form, they are not permitted to receive the bhikṣu precepts.

Nāgas and animals possess supernatural powers; they are not permitted to receive the precepts. Those who have committed incest with their six types of close relatives are not permitted to receive the precepts.

The above cases all belong to the category of "grave obstacles" (*guru-vighna*). Regarding the thirteen types [of obstacles] mentioned below, these are referred to as the "sixteen minor prohibitions" (*laghu-pratibandha*).
First, regarding my late father’s life as a layman: one must examine in detail the names of the heterodox and orthodox teachings he was instructed in.

Regarding his renunciation of the world, one must distinguish between right and wrong concerning what dharma he received. Throughout one's life, when meeting others, one should address them by their two-character dharma name;

one must not address them as "little monk" and the like, thereby insulting the gate of the Buddha-dharma, nor address them as "so-and-so," "you," "I," and so forth. One must recognize and avoid such proximate arrogance throughout one's career.

Who is it that is born? One is permitted to receive the full precepts only when twenty years of age are complete. One is permitted to receive the full precepts only when one’s own robes and bowl are fully provided.
One is permitted to receive the full precepts only when one has received the permission of one’s parents. One is permitted to receive the full precepts only when one does not owe debts to others.
A slave or servant of another is not permitted to receive the full precepts. An official serving the sacred court may not come to receive the bhikṣu precepts unless the King’s grace has been granted.

Regarding the precepts: those with illness are not permitted to leave the household life or receive the precepts. The "five illnesses" referred to here are scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, white leprosy, consumption, and insanity.

These constitute the sixteen minor prohibitions (*āvaraṇa*). Each must be scrutinized; furthermore, one’s conduct and understanding must be examined. Leaving the household life is a matter of great importance and must not be undertaken lightly.

Only after investigation and discernment in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings may one be permitted to proceed to the reception of the precepts. Once the examination is concluded, [the assembly]...
The ten masters shall act together. The preceptor shall privately question the candidate regarding their transgressions, observing whether they exist and their relative gravity.

If there is an obstruction, the conferral of the precepts is not permitted; furthermore, one should have them repent and prostrate before the thousand Buddhas of the three periods to benefit their advancement toward the precepts, so that prior karma may be extinguished and they may attain awakening.
Next, one should confer the Bodhisattva precepts upon them, provided there is no obstruction. If there is no obstruction...
If there are those who have committed minor offenses, they are instructed to perform prostrations and repentance, and to maintain purity through the recitation of mantras.

This is done out of concern that the śrāmaṇeras may not understand the Buddha’s era of begging for food, sleeping under trees, wearing robes made of discarded rags, using medicinal decoctions, and possessing few desires.
The Dharma of contentment leads to study. In these times, there is the fault of those who favor idleness, seek only security, and avoid the world while consuming food in excess;
therefore, one must first cause them to rely upon these four matters before conferring the precepts to become a Great Monk (*bhikṣu*).
First, appoint an *ācārya* to explain the *śrāmaṇera* precepts. This refers to the *śrāmaṇera* precepts conferred at the time of tonsure, which remain incomplete during the intervening period.
The practice has been mixed and impure; now, as you are about to receive the full precepts (*mahāśīla*), you shall finally enter the true stage of a *śrāmaṇera*.

First, a *ācārya* shall be appointed to instruct you in the methods for wearing the robes and using the alms bowl. These methods are vast, encompassing the principles of the Chan school and the doctrinal teachings, and cannot be mastered in a single day.
However, you should begin by applying yourself to what is used in daily life, first learning the proper deportment (*īryāpatha*), and gradually transforming yourself through these details.
The Guide: A single Acharya instructs the śrāmaṇera to arouse the superior-grade mind and ascend to the superior-grade precepts.

This is because, although the śrāmaṇera has stilled the mind to participate in the fundamental and give rise to the application of compassion, he is still but a fledgling of the Buddha and is not yet capable of the great function.
I now wish to bestow upon you, bhikṣu and seeker of the Dharma, the precepts that terrify Māra.

Although you have entered the vehicle of the śrāvaka with a pure physical basis, you must know that you possess the aspiration to ascend toward Buddhahood for the benefit of sentient beings; thus, you shall not remain settled in the erroneous views of the Hīnayāna.
Therefore, one should exert effort to cause the sprout of Buddhahood to grow so as not to let it wither and perish.

First, appoint an ācārya to establish the maṇḍala and perform the ritual procedures, knowing the format for bestowing the precepts. Second, the formal bestowal of the precepts. Third, appoint an ācārya to explain the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*).
Fourth, appoint an ācārya to instruct in the recitation of the precepts; thereafter, provide a detailed exposition of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The *Tripiṭaka*—specifically the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*—has already been clarified. Upon examining the various Vinayas extensively, regarding the bestowal of the Bodhisattva precepts:
in bestowing the great Bodhisattva precepts, one must not discriminate against the individual's character. One should simply observe their spiritual capacity (*indriya*).

Whether they have a sincere heart for practicing Chan, seek to realize *bodhi* through the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), sincerely aspire to be born in the Pure Land, or truly intend to propagate the teachings and benefit sentient beings, or perhaps establish [monasteries]...
Practices such as releasing living beings in forest monasteries are truly expedient means for those who forget themselves for the sake of others, not for those seeking fame or profit.

However, one should confer the full precepts upon anyone who understands the meaning of the phrases regarding the Dharma Master emitting light and offering flowers, provided they are free from the seven grave offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*).
These seven grave offenses are: shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, and killing one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
To murder one's own preceptor; to destroy the Saṃgha that performs the *karmavācanā* or turns the Wheel of Dharma; and to murder a noble being (*ārya*).
These are the cases that must be excluded; they are not permitted to receive the precepts.

As for all others—whether kings, princes, ministers, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, laywomen, male or female libertines, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the six classes of desire-realm devas, those lacking sexual organs, or those with two [sexual organs]—[none of these are excluded].
Those who are eunuchs, slaves, spirits, or animals may all receive the precepts.

A bhikṣu, wearing robes of the prescribed discolored hue and appearing in accordance with the Way, shall confer the Bodhisattva Great Precepts upon the fourfold assembly of renunciants. At all times, they must not be separated from those robes.

Once the great resolve has been generated and the necessary clothing and requisites are complete, one should enter [the retreat] no later than fifteen days or seven days prior to the scheduled date for the conferral of the precepts.
Regarding the period for receiving the teachings: as with the two assemblies of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, one must first undergo examination.

Only when one has completed the recitation of the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra* from back to front and possesses no deficiency in the fundamental precepts shall one be permitted to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Furthermore, in recent times, it is not permissible for bhikṣuṇīs to enter among the male assembly;
lest there be confusion, a separate expedient must be established. First, an ācārya is appointed to examine and verify that the candidate is indeed a bhikṣu.
For the two hundred and fifty precepts: one ācārya is appointed to recite the Three Refuges for both monastics and laypeople, causing them to know the method of Zen meditation;
one ācārya is appointed to conduct a formal inquiry regarding the seven obstacles (*saptāvaraṇa*);
one ācārya is appointed to explain the rite of repentance, causing them to repent their prior transgressions with a sincere mind; one ācārya is appointed to explain...
The Dharma of Ascetic Practice: to cause [the candidate] to know that they are a person who has forgotten the self; first, appoint an ācārya to exhort them to give rise to the Four Great Vows;
second, formally confer the Bodhisattva Mahā-śīla; third, appoint an ācārya to instruct them in the method of reciting the precepts.
Thereafter, he was instructed in the two fascicles of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* until he attained mastery. Next, he studied the Mahāyāna Vinaya-piṭaka.
For anyone who has left the household life, there is no principle by which the Bodhisattva precepts can be conferred directly; one must necessarily progress from the stages of śrāmaṇera and bhikṣu.
To leap over stages and advance recklessly is utterly contrary to the Buddha’s intention.
Even one with the Mahayana capacity such as the Great Master Huineng first received the bhikṣu precepts before opening the Dongshan Dharma-gate to benefit sentient beings.
For lay practitioners, however, the path proceeds from the five precepts up to the bodhisattva precepts; they do not follow the aforementioned precedent.
Chapter Twenty-Six: The Total Retention of Robe and Alms Bowl.
Now, the Buddha-mind has no conceptual meaning; the Buddha-dharma is beyond words. The Way is not distant from people; it is people themselves who do not investigate or awaken to it.
Thus, though one is constantly within this Way—putting on robes and eating meals—one forgets the original face in every single matter. Why is this so?
This is indeed so. It is because one employs conceptualization and discrimination throughout various situations, using the mouth to preach and explain;
for this reason, the mind that possesses the meaning beyond words is extinguished and vanishes.

Therefore, when thousands or tens of thousands of Buddhas appear in the world, they do not exert even a single hair’s breadth of effort to manifest through words and meanings; they simply transmit a single *pātra* and the three pieces of robe-cloth.
This is the Buddha’s Mind-Seal Wisdom. If a person attains it, there is not a single dharma that does not flow forth from the realm of food and clothing.
The Confucian says: "The Way cannot be left for even a moment; that which can be left is not the Way. One must simply awaken to this in the state where there is neither seeing nor hearing;
then, without the exertion of vigilance and fear, natural vigilance and fear will enter of their own accord.
One does not attain it for oneself. The *pātra* (alms bowl) refers to that which is eaten through right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). The robe refers to the ritual deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Right livelihood is that which cannot be attained within the Buddha-mind; deportment is the Dharma of the Buddha. The mind is that which has been one’s own fundamental ground from the beginning, within the sphere of every person;
to awaken to this is called fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Deportment is likewise within the sphere of every person.
One awakens to the patterns of every single act and movement; thus, from the very root, they flow forth, revealing the majestic light and ritual of the perfectly complete True Dharma.
What is the meaning of *pātra*? It is because the human fundamental mind is a great circle—black on the outside and empty within.
That which is circular is inherently perfect; there is no phenomenon it does not encompass. As for the black, it signifies... [the realization of] clarity.
Without mental activity, the essence is utterly extinguished. Emptiness is bottomless and boundless; what dharma is there that does not flow forth from it or reside within its containment?
Yet, when this single dharma is pointed out face-to-face, it leaves no room for even the great wisdom of all Buddhas.
It is perfectly integrated and profoundly deep, encompassing all things like the Unpolarized and Polarized Ultimate (Wuji and Taiji) before they have yet been differentiated in the *I Ching*.
Regarding that matter, even Fuxi and Confucius could not lay their hands upon it; yet, it is not a method of stifling death.
Thus, one closes while two open, branching out into many schools of Daoxue (Scholarly Learning). This is precisely like picking up a bowl.
This mind-ground is not stagnant water; from within a single hair’s breadth, it surges forth immeasurable Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
From the edges corresponding to the base and the cover, the Infinite (Wuji) and the Great Ultimate (Taiji) emerge and interact with one another. From this, they subsequently divide:

above becomes the Origin of Qian (Heaven), below becomes the Origin of Kun (Earth), and the center becomes the Great Void (Taixu). The Great Void is not empty; it thus becomes the Origin of Humanity (Ren).

The Origin of Humanity is the root of Heaven and Earth, which refers to that which existed prior to the very beginning. This is precisely what is meant by "Right Life-Sustenance" (Zhengming Shi). This...
One becomes two; two become three. The whole bowl is like a single phrase in the Chan school.

It encompasses the merging of guest and host, the interplay of ruler and minister, the harmony of father and son, and the seamless integration of phenomenon and principle. From this point on, the opening of a single thread begins.
Next, the three-legged stand of the bowl is contained within the great bowl itself; this is precisely the "single phrase" of the Chan school.

Within this, there are the three mysteries and three essentials, the three phrases of the mysterious path, the bird-track, the extended hand, the casket covering heaven and earth, cutting off all streams, following the waves, the stage of faith, the stage of persons, and the stage of no-position.
There is the single mind and the three contemplations, the self-returning to the Triple Gem and the Three Virtues, and so forth.
The three bowls together with the original great bowl make four; these four represent the guest and host, the fourfold discernment.
The four dharma-realms (dharmadhātu) are these four equal dharmas. This fundamental wisdom is the great dharma that fully embodies the essence of the mind.
However, to have the bowl without the robe means the dharma is incomplete. If the dharma is incomplete, the mind is incomplete; therefore, the robe begins with five strips.
This is like the Five Ranks of Master and Subject or the Five Ranks of Prince and Heir in the Chan school; in Confucianism, it is as follows:
The numbers of the five heavens and the five earths constitute twenty-five. In terms of the teachings, this refers to the division into five periods, five teachings, and five flavors.
These five categories correspond to the number five; within these numbers lies the essence of numbering. Therefore, it causes the monk to wear the robe by attaching it to his body.
Each strip has one long and one short side; the cutting represents the mutual interplay of the partial and the correct.
This is the root. The marvelous Yang (Yang) gives birth to life. Beginning from the one bowl, it proceeds through the three bowls;
then to the five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-one, twenty-three, twenty-five, and finally thirty-five strips of the robe.
Furthermore, there is the five-strip robe with ten intervals, called the *kāṭhina* robe. All of these directly demonstrate the Dharma.
It is a matter of number. Regarding the seven-strip robe (*saptaka-cīvara*), based on the size of the alms bowl, four units constitute the four borders of the five-strip robe;
by adding three to those four, it becomes seven. The number seven resides within five; this increase in number represents the growth of the Yang (the creative force).

In the Chan school, the seven items carried with one’s person are the ritual protocol for practicing the Way. In the Exoteric Teachings (*kyō*), they correspond to the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-sambodhy-aṅga*) and the seven noble riches (*sapta-ārya-dhana*), and so forth.

Furthermore, two [panels] are long and one is short; they are inverted and interchanged, such that the long ones predominate and the short ones are few. This is the sign of the increase of the noble (ārya) and the decrease of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
This is the standard appearance of the robe worn when entering the assembly, known as the *antarvāsaka* (inner robe).

Starting from nine strips, it represents the old age of the yang number; thus, it is the beginning of the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe). Among the numbers of the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*), encountering ten signifies death, while encountering nine—
Thus it arises. This is why the Luo Shu (River Chart) takes nine as the divine function of unfathomable transformation.
Therefore, in the method of Linji, a single phrase contains the three mysteries, and within each mystery there are the three essentials; this is the principle of the five ranks of ruler and minister.
This is also the intended meaning of dividing the five stages by means of four dharmas. In terms of the teachings, this refers to breaking down the nine marks and realizing that they are ignorance.
Including the eleven and thirteen strips, these are all considered the lower grade. The fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen strips of the great robe (saṃghāṭī) constitute the middle grade.
As for the great robe made of cut-and-sewn pieces with three lengths and one shortness, the more strips there are, [the higher the grade].
The Way becomes increasingly superior. Those with twenty-one strips, twenty-three strips, and twenty-five strips constitute the upper-grade *saṃghāṭī*.
Each consists of four lengths and one short piece, thus fulfilling the number five. Indeed, the numbers proceed from five;

five times five makes twenty-five, which is the ultimate of the yang numbers. Thus, the five robes symbolize the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), while the seven robes symbolize the stage of abiding (*vihāra*).
The stages: the three robes being worn as a full set represent the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).

The three robes being entirely unattached, like a lotus flower, represent the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*). These all signify the wisdom of differentiation (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*). This sequence proceeds from the alms bowl to the robes.
The two fundamental wisdoms of differentiation reach their perfection here. Twenty-five is the odd number; fifty-five is the combination of odd and even.
Thus, the five lines and ten divisions encompass them. The four conditions are the yang numbers; twenty-five is the yin number.
Thirty is represented by leaving one position empty to form an image. These fifty-five positions constitute the true path to Bodhi. [This is] the dyed color.
These [colors] are not the primary colors of the five directions. Generally speaking, primary colors belong to principle (*li*). Principle encompasses both word and meaning;

this Dharma ought to be expressed beyond words, and thus it yields to the primary colors. As for worldly dharmas, such as Mount Sumeru, the sun, and the moon, their manifestations are fully present within the patterns of the robes.
It can be seen that from the entry of an ordinary person into sainthood, all the way until the attainment of Buddhahood, depends solely upon these two matters: the alms bowl and the robe.
Seeing this and beholding it, how could one not cultivate and realize it? Having fully mastered the use of this robe and this bowl, how could they be separated from the body for even a moment?
Therefore, it is called "the field of merit. Both mundane and supramundane blessings are all generated and nurtured from this.
To awaken to this, to know this, and to act in reliance upon this—this alone is wisdom. It is like a field being irrigated with water.

It moistens and nourishes the sprouts. Therefore, every thread of the robe is permeated with waterways, symbolizing that both the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) are made to flow and irrigate continuously.
This is the sublime Dharma of the supramundane; it is the food of right livelihood and the robe of the sublime Dharma and right livelihood.
If one wears this correctly, the Buddhas of the three periods of time have no way to emerge from it. This is the Dharma.

This is its essence. If one sees people or sees the Buddha, and there is an occasion where conditions respond, then one should manifest a partial attachment—revealing a single thread of the Way—to cause others to awaken.
Apart from this, the wondrous function of mutual interpenetration is not something reached through deep awakening; it is not understood even by those who have studied for a long time.
Disciples of the Buddha, you should accord with the Dharma of the robe and wear it at all times, just as a Confucianist studies and practices it constantly. At all times...
In the midst of this, one becomes unaware and unconscious, growing so habituated that the method is forgotten.
Once the method is forgotten, amidst one’s deportment, there is naturally a dignified composure, radiating a brilliant luster like a thousand-acre pond brimming with water;
its moistening brilliance is like the "Joy" (Sui) hexagram—this is precisely what the Confucianist means by the phrase, "Is this not joy? (ruo bu ye shuo hu zhi yi).
It is the same. Entering through such awakening, practicing in such a manner, and attaining such mastery, one acts spontaneously without deliberate thought.
Like voices responding to one another and like kind natures seeking each other out, friends come from afar to sing in harmony with the Great Way of Bodhi.
Unconsciously, this Way flows forth and transforms all; naturally, the hawks soar and the fish leap. The Confucians say: "Is it not joyful?"

Ah! True joy is not something possessed by the mind; if there were a mind [grasping it], it would not be true joy. This is one who internally perfects the Buddha-mind and externally propagates the Buddha-way.

If he were to live in an age of the Final Dharma when heterodox teachings prevail, and people—failing to recognize the direct pointing of the almsbowl—instead regarded him as having strange speech and strange dress, and thus rejected and ostracized him, then such a thing would indeed be appropriate.
Resentment arises from within. This refers to one who is in accord with the robe and bowl; such a person’s joy is not of the mind, for their source of happiness is inherently autonomous.
Thus, even when encountering the perils of the Dharma, they fundamentally have no such [resentful] intent, and therefore feel no resentment. In Confucian terms, this is a "junzi" (gentleman);
in Buddhist terms, this is a true son of the Buddha. With the three robes and a single bowl, face covered in dust and head smeared with ash, they withdraw from the world.
If one does not employ the mind of seeing and knowing as an active function, then naturally there will be no cause for regret.
In this Way, one also does not lose the great banner of radiant light. This is a mechanism that neither ordinary beings nor sages can fathom.
As for the robe and the bowl—can they not be received and held perpetually?
